bioinfo.title: CardamomOT: A mechanistic optimal transport-based framework for gene regulatory network inference, trajectory reconstruction and generative modeling.
bioinfo.abstract: A key challenge in inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs) governing cellular processes such as differentiation and reprogramming from experimental data lies in the impossibility of directly measuring protein dynamics at the single-cell level, which prevents establishing causal relationships between regulator activity and target responses. In earlier work, we introduced CARDAMOM, an algorithm that uses temporal snapshots of scRNA-seq data to calibrate a GRN-driven mechanistic model of gene expression. However, this method had several limitations: it could only rely on the relative ordering of time points rather than their exact labels, imposed restrictive quasi-stationary assumptions on protein dynamics, and depended on multiple hyperparameters. Here, we present CardamomOT, a new method based on the same mechanistic model that jointly reconstructs the GRN and unobserved protein trajectories from the data within a mechanistic optimal transport framework. By incorporating exact time labels and priors on protein kinetic rates from the literature, and substantially reducing the number of required hyperparameters, our approach addresses these limitations and substantially improves the accuracy and robustness of GRN calibration. We validate our framework on both in silico and experimental datasets, demonstrating computational scalability and consistently improved performance over state-of-the-art methods in both GRN and trajectory reconstruction on simulated datasets, and, on experimental datasets, reconstruction of cellular trajectories, velocity fields and latent protein levels that are mutually consistent, together with GRN structures consistent with known biology. We also show that these improvements make the calibrated mechanistic model suitable to be used as a generative model to generate testable predictions of cellular responses to unseen perturbations. To our knowledge, this is among the first methods to explicitly integrate mechanistic GRN inference, trajectory reconstruction, and simulation of realistic datasets into a unified framework for scRNA-seq time series analysis.

bioinfo.title: MultiFlow: coupled flow matching for predicting single-cell multiomic perturbation responses in unseen cellular contexts
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Predicting cellular responses to perturbation requires resolving coordinated changes across molecular layers, yet most single-cell perturbation models focus on transcriptional responses alone. Here we present MultiFlow, a coupled flow-matching framework that unifies generation and perturbation prediction of paired gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Through bidirectional information exchange between RNA and ATAC generative flows, MultiFlow learns how their joint distribution depends on cellular context and perturbation identity. Across multiomic generation benchmarks, MultiFlow accurately reproduced paired RNA-ATAC states and their population distributions. In multiome perturbation benchmarks, MultiFlow achieved the strongest overall performance in predicting both gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility perturbation responses, outperforming modality-specific perturbation-prediction methods in cell types whose perturbed states were withheld from training. Joint multiomic modeling further preserved perturbation-induced coordination between modalities, including concordant peak-gene effects and cross-modal cellular neighborhood structure. These results establish MultiFlow as a unified generative framework for modeling paired molecular states and predicting their coordinated perturbation responses across cellular contexts. Code and tutorial of MultiFlow are available at https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow .

bioinfo.title: Synchronized Optimal Transport Reconstructs Coupled Transcriptomic and Chromatin Dynamics.
bioinfo.abstract: Single-cell RNA and ATAC data collected across developmental stages provide time-course snapshots of transcriptional and regulatory states. Since sequencing is destructive, trajectories between these snapshots must be inferred from independently sampled cell populations. Existing approaches typically infer continuous dynamics in a single modality or integrate RNA and ATAC in a shared representation. Here we present Cross-Omics Aligned Trajectory Inference (COATI), which extends unbalanced synchronized dynamical optimal transport to time-dependent cross-modal maps for reconstructing coupled trajectories in distinct RNA and ATAC state spaces. We evaluated COATI on synthetic benchmarks and four developmental datasets using held-out-stage reconstruction and lineage analyses. COATI improved reconstruction of cell populations at held-out stages, including recovery of chromatin-state heterogeneity within cell types, and better preserved developmental lineage relationships. The unbalanced formulation allows the inference of population mass changes, which were shown to associate with DNA-replication programs at early stages and lineage-maturation programs later in development. The coupled trajectories enabled analysis of lineage-specific transcriptional and chromatin changes and their temporal relationships during development. Lineage responses inferred by COATI agreed with independent CRISPR perturbation results, and the inferred regulatory patterns were consistent with independent epigenetic data.

bioinfo.title: MitoLODE: a virtual mitochondrion framework with knowledge graph priors for trajectory modeling and mechanistic perturbation analysis.
bioinfo.abstract: Mitochondria play a central role in the pathogenesis of major diseases. Tracking how they evolve under disease conditions is valuable for understanding pathological mechanisms and identifying intervention windows. Existing single-cell trajectory inference methods rely on pseudotime rather than a real temporal axis, and rarely model disease and control as independent trajectories. Virtual cell methods target one-shot drug perturbation responses and do not handle the continuous temporal evolution of disease phenotypes. To address these gaps, we propose a virtual mitochondrion research paradigm. We first curate and construct MitoKG, a mitochondria-specific heterogeneous knowledge graph integrated from five authoritative databases. MitoKG contains 2549 nodes of four types and 23 019 edges of five relation types. Building on these priors, we develop MitoLODE, a conditioned dual-trajectory neural ordinary differential equation framework. MitoLODE embeds graph priors and temporal features throughout encoding, continuous-time dynamics, and decoding, modeling disease and control evolution as two coupled paths. Benchmarked against eight baselines across four datasets covering Parkinson's disease, cardiac, and pancreatic differentiation, MitoLODE leads in most settings and remains robust under low-data regimes and extrapolation to unseen time points. Two synthetic datasets with known ground truth validate its trajectory recovery under controlled conditions. Building on the trained model, we design a gradient-guided perturbation procedure that identifies potential intervention targets aligned with known Parkinson's pathology. We develop MGMI, a large language model-based reasoning module that grounds model outputs in MitoKG nodes and turns them into confidence-graded mechanistic hypotheses, which nonetheless require experimental validation.

bioinfo.title: GeoSinkhorn Flow: Geometry-Aware Flow Matching for Perturbation-Conditioned Dynamics in Single cell Data Phenoscapes
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Single-cell technologies increasingly enable large-scale profiling of complex biological systems across many experimental perturbations, but understanding how a system reorganizes across an entire space of conditions is difficult to interpret from single-cell embeddings alone. Phenoscapes address this by embedding entire cell-state distributions, rather than individual cells, as points in a data-driven landscape. Thus, a single dot represents one experimental condition rather than one cell, yielding a map of the perturbation or patient landscape that reveals how phenotype varies continuously across conditions. Phenoscapes remain a comparatively new and underexplored representation and existing static phenoscapes position experimental conditions relative to one another without specifying trajectories that describe how a cellular population moves from one condition to another. Flow- and trajectory-based models for single-cell data are numerous, but existing approaches operate at the level of individual cells, are not built to respect the geometry of a phenoscape, and typically cannot generalize their predicted flows to conditions not seen during training. Here we introduce GeoSinkhorn Flow, a perturbation-conditioned, geometry-aware flow-matching framework specialized designed to convert a static phenoscape into a dynamic phenoscape, in which each condition-level point is additionally connected by geodesic, condition-aware transport trajectories that are consistent with the phenoscape’s underlying geometry. GeoSinkhorn Flow can also model transitions directly between time points without constructing a phenoscape. GeoSinkhorn Flow uses heat-diffusion geometry to define manifold-aware transport costs and trains a geometric autoencoder whose latent Euclidean distances stay aligned with the static phenoscape geometry while extending it to unseen cells. By explicitly conditioning the learned transport dynamics on perturbation-specific gene or drug embeddings, GeoSinkhorn Flow generalizes its trajectories to new measurement conditions, produces intermediate progression states along a trajectory, and extends predictions to unseen cells and held-out perturbations. An unbalanced optimal transport variant further learns growth or transition weights, so that changes in relative cell-state abundance or transition propensity are modeled together with state movement. Across synthetic manifolds, patient-derived organoid drug responses, Perturb-seq knockdowns, and time-resolved CyTOF signaling, GeoSinkhorn Flow recovered intrinsic manifold geometry, inferred biologically coherent response trajectories, and generalized to held-out drug combinations, perturbation genes, and time points. Together, these results establish GeoSinkhorn Flow as a perturbation-conditioned, phenoscape-consistent dynamical framework, distinct from standard flow-matching approaches, for converting static phenoscapes into dynamic ones that generalize across experimental conditions. Abstract Figure Overview of the GeoSinkhorn Flow pipeline. a) Single-cell measurements under control and perturbation conditions. b) Static phenoscape: each condition is one point representing its full cell distribution, and distances are Geodesic Sinkhorn (geodesic optimal transport) distances. c) Dynamic phenoscape: perturbation-conditioned trajectories carry the control population to each perturbation, and each trajectory is conditioned on its perturbation embedding c k . The inset shows single-cell trajectories under f θ ( z, c 1 , t ). d) Perturbation conditioning: drug and gene embeddings, with combinations composed from single agents, condition a flow over latent cell state z and progression t . This lets a single model predict a distinct trajectory for each perturbation, including held-out combinations (dashed).

bioinfo.title: Efficient Bayesian inference for ordinary differential equation models from experimental data with uncertain measurement times
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Time-resolved measurements are central to calibrating mechanistic dynamical models, but current inference frameworks typically assume that reported measurement times are exact. In practice, actual sampling times may deviate from reported times because of sample-handling delays, imper-fect synchronization, or reporting errors. Here, we present a Bayesian framework for parameter inference in ordinary differential equation models that explicitly accounts for uncertainty in measurement times. We formulate latent measurement times as random variables and derive a joint and marginalized posterior. To compute the marginal likelihood efficiently, we augment the original dynamical system with additional state variables that evaluate the required integrals during numerical simulation. This reduces the dimensionality of the estimation problems and allows for efficient and reliable Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. Across synthetic examples and a published model of carotenoid cleavage in Arabidopsis thaliana , neglecting time uncertainty led to biased estimates and overconfident uncertainty quantification, whereas the proposed marginalized formulation recovered reliable parameter estimates while substantially improving sampling efficiency and scalability. These results identify measurement time uncertainty as an important source of variability in dynamic modeling and establish posterior marginalization as a practical strategy for robust mechanistic inference.

bioinfo.title: SPARC Reveals Distinct Osteoclastogenesis-Associated Malignant States in Metastatic Osteosarcoma.
bioinfo.abstract: Single-cell studies of metastatic cancer have revealed extensive transcriptional heterogeneity and cellular plasticity as malignant populations establish themselves in distant organs. The growing availability of paired single-cell profiles from primary tumors and matched metastases offers new opportunities to investigate how malignant-cell states evolve during metastasis in relation to progression within the primary tumor. Static comparisons between these sites have identified differences in cellular composition and molecular programs, but can reduce heterogeneous populations to site-level summaries and overlook changes in gene-expression programs along possible routes of metastatic progression. Investigating these dynamics calls for trajectory inference that reconstructs state progression within each condition and transitions between conditions. However, existing trajectory inference tools have limitations in jointly modeling these relationships under biological ordering constraints. Traditional and widely used trajectory inference tools, such as Monocle 3 and Slingshot, do not impose direction constraints based on biological knowledge or the sampling design during graph construction. Optimal transport-based tools, such as moscot, incorporate temporal order to infer cross-condition correspondences, but these mappings alone do not reconstruct progression within each condition. More recent methods, including CStreet and CellRank 2, incorporate both transition types, but construct the two components separately through distinct modeling or graph-construction strategies. Here we introduce SPARC (Shortest Path Algorithmic Reconstruction of Cross-state Evolution), a unified graph-based optimization framework that evaluates both types of relationships under a common connectivity formulation to reconstruct complete, directionally constrained candidate trajectories. Across benchmarks, SPARC improved recovery of candidate metastatic precursors and complete progression routes in simulations, showed strong directed-trajectory reconstruction in conventional time-course settings, and performed competitively in real tumor lineage-tracing datasets. To examine metastatic progression in a model where lung lesions arise through spontaneous dissemination, we generated, to our knowledge, the first paired scRNA-seq dataset of primary osteosarcoma tumors and spontaneous lung metastases from the same mice, together with the first patient-derived osteosarcoma Visium HD dataset. The biological analyses revealed differences among metastatic tumor states in their association with osteoclast-like myeloid populations and candidate supportive signals, suggesting that certain malignant states may preferentially promote osteoclastogenesis. Together, SPARC provides a framework for investigating biologically ordered cell-state progression and identifying state-specific programs associated with metastatic disease.

bioinfo.title: Bridging Graph and Pairwise Learning for Gene Regulatory Network Inference from scRNA-seq Data.
bioinfo.abstract: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) capture the underlying interactions through which transcription factors (TFs) regulate genes. Based on gene expression data, existing GRN inference approaches generally fall into two categories: graph-based methods, which model the GRN as a whole graph, and pairwise-based methods, which decompose the GRN into individual TF-target gene pairs for modeling. However, each approach exhibits limitations that are precisely the strengths of its counterpart. Graph-based methods tend to overfit due to their reliance on a single training graph, whereas pairwise-based methods benefit from abundant TF-target training pairs. In contrast, pairwise-based methods overlook the global topological structure, which is essential for comprehensively capturing regulatory mechanisms. To address these limitations, we propose scGPL, an end-to-end unified framework that jointly models global regulatory topology and local interactions. scGPL extracts macro-level features from the global regulatory graph and introduces a dynamic, importance-guided subgraph sampling mechanism to capture fine-grained local dependencies. By fusing global representations with subgraph-enhanced local features, our framework bridges the gap between the two paradigms, incorporating essential whole-graph topological dependencies while retaining the data abundance advantage of pairwise methods. Extensive experiments on seven benchmark datasets demonstrate that scGPL consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance, with up to 13.7% improvement over the strongest baseline, validating the effectiveness of our integrative design. The source code is maintained on GitHub (https://github.com/talent-hang/scGPL), and the datasets and versioned releases are archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21608485 for reproducibility.

bioinfo.title: Predicting the unseen: A diffusion-based debiasing framework for transcriptional response prediction at single-cell resolution
bioinfo.abstract: Predicting cellular responses to genetic perturbations is critical for advancing our understanding of gene regulation. While single-cell CRISPR perturbation assays such as Perturb-seq provide direct measurements of gene function, the scale of these experiments is limited by cost and feasibility. This motivates the development of computational approaches that can accurately infer responses to unmeasured perturbations from related experimental data. We introduce dbDiffusion, a generative framework that integrates diffusion models with classifier-free guidance derived from perturbation information, operating in latent space through a variational autoencoder. Diffusion models are probabilistic generative models that approximate data distributions by reversing a Markovian diffusion process, progressively denoising Gaussian noise into structured outputs. By exploiting biological similarities in gene expression profiles and relationships among perturbations, dbDiffusion enables the conditional generation of gene expressions for previously unobserved perturbations. In contrast to competing approaches, dbDiffusion does not rely on Large Language Model or foundation models, which have been found to yield unsatisfactory results. Rather, it leverages embeddings derived from measured perturbations to generalize to unseen perturbations, effectively transferring information across related experimental conditions. In benchmarking against state-of-the-art methods on Perturb-seq datasets, dbDiffusion demonstrates superior accuracy in predicting perturbation responses. A methodological innovation of dbDiffusion is the integration of prediction-powered inference, which corrects for biases inherent in generative models and enables statistically rigorous downstream tasks, including the identification of differentially expressed genes. By combining deep generative modeling with principled inference, dbDiffusion establishes a scalable computational framework for predicting and analyzing transcriptomic perturbation responses, significantly extending the utility of Perturb-seq experiments.

bioinfo.title: CeSpGRN: inferring cell-specific gene regulatory networks from single-cell multi-omics and spatial data.
bioinfo.abstract:
Motivation

Single-cell sequencing technologies allow researchers to study cell-cell variation within a cell population. Variations between cells are driven by the underlying biological network, particularly gene regulatory networks (GRNs). GRNs rewire as cells evolve, and different cells can have different GRNs. However, while single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell multi-omics data have been used to reconstruct GRNs, the output GRNs are rarely cell-specific, but rather, most existing methods infer population-level or cell-type-level GRNs.

Results

We propose CeSpGRN (Cell-Specific Gene Regulatory Network inference), a method that infers cell-specific GRNs from scRNA-seq, paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq, or spatial transcriptomic data. In particular, existing methods that use matching scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data incorporate population-level region information in GRN inference, whereas CeSpGRN utilizes single-cell resolution region information. CeSpGRN infers cell-specific GRNs using a kernel-weighted Gaussian Copula Graphical Model, and incorporates multi-omic or spatial location information when constructing the objective function. We tested CeSpGRN on both simulated and real datasets, and the results show that CeSpGRN has a superior performance compared to baseline methods in reconstructing GRNs and detecting regulatory interactions that differ between cells. CeSpGRN uncovered regulatory interactions that rewire during biological processes on real datasets.

Availability and implementation

CeSpGRN is a Python package available at https://github.com/PeterZZQ/CeSpGRN.

bioinfo.title: LoCoFlow: Local-Context Flow Matching for Single-Cell Dynamics and Fate Inference
bioinfo.abstract: A bstract Single-cell sequencing profiles cellular states at discrete time points, providing population-level snapshots from which developmental and disease-associated trajectories can be reconstructed. Existing optimal-transport and flow-matching approaches typically infer temporal couplings at the level of individual cells, with limited representation of the local manifold geometry of cell-state space and the uncertainty inherent in lineage diversification. We introduce LOCOFLOW, a flow-matching framework that combines local point-cloud geometry with conditional fate uncertainty. Overlapping patches define hierarchical transport between populations, and an endpoint-preserving neural bridge regularizes motion and deformation within these patches. Bridge velocities supervise a conditional field with patch-shared and cell-specific latent variables, from which alternative trajectories can be sampled without future observations. Temporal and spatial benchmarks show improvements in transport distance. On lineage-traced LARRY data, LO-COFLOW reduces mean raw Brier error from 0.7990 to 0.6620 relative to scDiffEq at the same number of endpoint draws. Expression perturbations further reveal distinct roles for focal-cell and neighborhood information: geometric-patch models show aligned background and whole-patch responses, whereas random-minibatch models show opposing focal and background responses. These findings support local context as a useful representation for probabilistic fate inference and provide testable hypotheses about how it shapes predicted responses.

bioinfo.title: BEAR-GRN: Systematic assessment of single-cell multi-omics-based gene regulatory network inference methods.
bioinfo.abstract: Identifying regulatory gene interactions is inherently challenging as it depends on both the transcriptional and epigenetic landscapes. Multiple methods are proposed to infer gene regulatory networks (GRNs) using single-cell multi-omics data, yet the absence of a standardized benchmarking framework remains an obstacle to unbiased performance evaluation. Here we present BEAR-GRN, a systematic resource providing standardized datasets, curated ground-truth networks, and a unified computational pipeline for benchmarking GRN inference methods. Using BEAR-GRN, we assess state-of-the-art multi-omics GRN inference methods across paired single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq datasets spanning human and mouse cell types. We evaluate accuracy against four complementary ground-truth definitions, alongside computational efficiency, output stability, and modality contribution. Although ground-truth choice profoundly influences performance, LINGER and DIRECT-NET show the highest overall accuracy and stability. Modality perturbation experiments reveal that current methods are predominantly RNA-driven, with chromatin accessibility contributing limited independent signal. BEAR-GRN enables researchers to evaluate existing and new GRN methods against established baselines.

bioinfo.title: scMomer: a pretraining framework for inferring robust cellular representations from single-cell transcriptomes
bioinfo.abstract: High-quality cellular representations are important for understanding complex biological systems. However, due to limitations in both data availability and practical utility, most existing computational methods are designed for a single modality (e.g., scRNA-seq or scATAC-seq), restricting their ability to capture cellular heterogeneity. Here, we propose scMomer, a multistage pretraining framework designed to infer robust cellular representations by integrating multimodal knowledge into scRNA-seq-only inputs. The framework progressively learns through three stages. Firstly, it pretrains unimodal encoders on single-modality datasets to obtain modality-specific representations. Secondly, it aligns these modalities using paired data to learn joint representations. Thirdly, it applies knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge of the missing modality (scATAC-seq) into a cross-modal student encoder, enabling the inference of multimodal-aware representations from scRNA-seq-only inputs. We perform extensive experiments show that the representations learned by scMomer achieve superior performance compared with state-of-the-art methods across diverse tasks, including cross-modality translation, cell annotation, drug response prediction, perturbation prediction, and gene property prediction, demonstrating its robustness and versatility. Overall, we demonstrate that scMomer enables unimodal data to yield robust cellular representations, providing an effective solution to missing-modality modeling.

bioinfo.title: CHAMPOLLION: Robust Multi-Omics Integration via Inverse Optimal Transport Using Paired Cells
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Fully capturing cellular identity requires integrating multiple molecular layers. Bridge integration, i.e. aligning unimodal datasets using a paired multi-omic reference, has emerged as a practical solution, yet existing methods offer limited interpretability and use paired information without regularization, making them sensitive to limited size and coverage. We introduce CHAMPOLLION, which uses regularized optimal transport to learn an interpretable cross-modal metric that drives the alignment of unpaired cells while capturing relationships between molecular features. Benchmarks on RNA-protein and RNA-ATAC datasets show that CHAMPOLLION outperforms existing approaches, remaining accurate with few paired cells and even generalizing to unseen cell types. Beyond alignment, CHAMPOLLION reveals biologically meaningful cross-modal relationships, highlighting in scRNA-protein data a potential role for CD18 across multiple cancers, and, in a human tonsil atlas combining scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq, suggesting that MEF2C may regulate inflammatory responses beyond the brain, notably in plasmacytoid dendritic cells.

bioinfo.title: velotest: statistical assessment of RNA velocity embeddings reveals quality differences for reliable trajectory visualizations.
bioinfo.abstract: Contemporary single-cell RNA-sequencing studies typically use RNA velocity analyses to investigate cellular dynamics. Commonly, RNA velocities are assessed with two-dimensional projections. Although it is well established that nonlinear embeddings of gene expression data cannot comprehensively preserve the structure of the original high-dimensional data across scales, there is no tool that systematically assesses and quantifies the faithfulness of velocity embeddings. This situation potentially leads to misleading velocity visualizations and putative cell state transitions. To this end, we introduce velotest, a cell-level statistical test that quantifies the faithfulness of a velocity embedding with respect to its high-dimensional counterpart. Applying velotest across multiple datasets and embedding methods, we find strong differences in the embedding qualities between embedding methods, datasets, and regions in individual datasets. velotest thus provides an essential validation step and enables researchers to select a suitable visualization of high-dimensional velocities, ensuring that hypotheses drawn from velocity projections are grounded in accurately represented dynamics.

bioinfo.title: Decomposing multi-scale dynamic regulation from single-cell multiomics with scMagnify.
bioinfo.abstract: Deciphering the highly coupled regulatory circuits that drive cellular dynamics remains a fundamental goal in biology. However, capturing the multi-scale time-lagged dynamics and combinatorial regulatory logic of gene regulation remains challenging. Here we present scMagnify, a deep-learning-based framework that leverages chromatin accessibility and gene expression via Granger causality to reconstruct and decompose multi-scale gene regulatory networks (GRNs). Diverse benchmarks demonstrate scMagnify's favorable performance. scMagnify employs tensor decomposition to identify combinatorial TF modules and their activation profiles across multiple time-lags. We applied scMagnify to human hematopoiesis and mouse pancreas development, where it recovered known lineage-driving regulators and provided further insights into the combinatorial logic underlying cell fate decisions. Furthermore, in the context of kidney injury, scMagnify's intercellular communication module mapped key signaling-to-transcription cascades linking microenvironment cues to pathological epithelial cell changes. In summary, scMagnify provides a robust computational framework for dissecting the multi-scale regulatory logic that governs complex biological processes in development and disease.

bioinfo.title: Integrative graph deep learning with directional decoding for robust gene regulatory network inference from single-cell transcriptomics.
bioinfo.abstract: While gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are fundamental to understanding complex cellular mechanisms, the accurate inference from single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data is hindered by the inherent noise, transcriptional dropout events, and dynamic nature of gene regulation. Current computational approaches often overlook long-range regulatory interactions, lack explicit modeling of regulatory directionality, and suffer from limited generalizability. To address these limitations, we introduce scGRAIL, a supervised deep learning framework that combines inductive local-aware graph aggregation (LGA) with an asymmetric relation decoder to enable robust GRN inference. Within this framework, LGA performs multi-hop neighborhood aggregation on a transcription factor (TF)-target graph, jointly leveraging topological structure and gene expression to capture long-range regulatory dependencies. A node reconstruction autoencoder (NAE) imposes gene expression reconstruction constraints on the latent embeddings, thereby enhancing robustness to noise and data heterogeneity and improving generalization. An asymmetric difference mechanism is introduced during decoding for distinct modeling of TFs and target genes; by computing an ordered difference vector between their embeddings, the model explicitly captures the directionality and target specificity of TF-target regulatory interactions, facilitating more accurate identification of potential causal regulatory relationships. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate the model's superiority: it achieves optimal performance on 86.4% of benchmark datasets (38/44), surpassing state-of-the-art methods. Notably, scGRAIL achieves a 4.25% increase in average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) across four real-world networks compared to the graph contrastive link prediction (GCLink) model, yielding a 17.64% AUROC improvement for the TF500+ Non-Specific network in the mouse hematopoietic stem cells with lymphoid-lineage (mHSC-L) dataset, demonstrating its resilience to noise and scalability for large-scale GRNs. These results establish scGRAIL as a transformative tool for uncovering gene regulatory logic in single-cell transcriptomics. Overall, scGRAIL enhances structural modeling and directional discrimination in single-cell GRN inference by using multi-hop graph aggregation to capture long-range regulatory dependencies, expression reconstruction constraints to improve cross-dataset robustness, and an asymmetric decoding mechanism to explicitly model the regulatory directionality between TFs and target genes.

bioinfo.title: LOTUS: lineage-aware optimal transport reconstructs continuous clonal fate dynamics
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Destructive sampling in single-cell sequencing obscures ancestor–descendant relationships, limiting the continuous reconstruction of cell-fate dynamics. Here we present Lineage-aware optimal transport for unbalanced single-cell dynamics (LOTUS), a framework that integrates time-resolved transcriptomic snapshots with clonal lineage information from engineered barcodes or endogenous T cell receptor clonotypes. LOTUS couples clone-level optimal transport with neural unbalanced transport to model continuous cellular state change, population growth and clonal propagation under lineage-consistent constraints. In branching simulations, LOTUS reduced lineage-inconsistent transport relative to benchmark methods, lowering off-target routing from 4.94–14.84% to 1.10%. On LARRY lineage-barcode scRNA-seq of hematopoiesis, LOTUS reconstructed branching trajectories, improved early neutrophil–monocyte fate-boundary prediction, and inferred multi-fate progenitors and fate-biased meta-clones, linking their distinct fate potentials to inferred epigenetic priming. On CellTagging scRNA-seq of fibroblast reprogramming, it distinguished reprogrammed from failed trajectories and prioritized fate-associated perturbation genes. In longitudinal scRNA-seq and TCR-seq of malaria-responsive memory (CD45RA-) CD4+ T cells, it preserved endogenous clonotype structure and reconstructed TR1 dynamics and regulatory networks. LOTUS thus converts lineage-resolved single-cell snapshots into interpretable, continuous models of fate dynamics and their regulatory programs.

bioinfo.title: scUnify: a unified framework for training and inference across multiple single-cell foundation models
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) differ in software requirements and performance across downstream tasks and adaptation strategies, complicating comparison and reuse. We present scUnify, a framework that preserves each backbone’s required processing while separating model-specific trainers, downstream tasks, and adaptation strategies as reusable components. Across five scFMs, scUnify reproduced original inference and training workflows, extended model-native tasks with multiple parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, and demonstrated extensibility by connecting a newly implemented custom trainable task to multiple backbones and adaptation strategies. Together, these capabilities enable researchers to systematically compare these combinations and extend custom tasks across heterogeneous scFMs within a common workflow.

bioinfo.title: A unified framework for scalable differential testing for spatial omics
Computational single-cell and spatial multi-omics approaches for decoding shared and disease-specific neuroimmune landscapes across brain disorders
bioinfo.abstract: Neuroinflammation contributes to pathogenesis across Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, ischemic stroke, and primary brain tumors, but single-cell and spatial transcriptomic atlases of these conditions have largely been analyzed in isolation, obscuring how these conditions engage shared versus disease-specific immunological programs. This review examines how computational frameworks for single-cell and spatial multi-omics analysis can identify shared and disease-specific neuroimmune patterns across brain disorders. Organized by analytical paradigm rather than by individual disease, the review covers data integration and cell-state annotation, trajectory inference, gene regulatory network reconstruction, spatial deconvolution, GWAS-to-cell-type mapping, and intercellular communication, drawing on cross-disease evidence from Alzheimer’s disease, glioma, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, and stroke. The evidence identifies four neuroinflammatory modules that recur across diagnostic boundaries, including disease-associated microglia (DAM) activation, interferon-stimulated gene responses, complement cascade reactivation, and metabolic reprogramming toward glycolysis. Despite this shared core, the tissue-level manifestation of these modules differs substantially across conditions, and the spatial architecture of immune cell organization is disease-specific. Translation of these findings is constrained by nomenclature fragmentation across independently defined microglial states, species discordance between mouse models and human tissue, underrepresentation of non-Alzheimer’s neurodegenerative and psychiatric disorders, and the near-complete absence of prospective clinical validation for computationally defined cell states. Addressing these gaps requires the field to advance from cataloguing cell states to cross-disease integrative frameworks with unified cell-state nomenclature, prospective validation in clinical cohorts, and analytical methods capable of distinguishing correlation from causation in neuroimmune cascades. This review provides a comparative framework for interpreting neuroimmune cell states across brain disorders and delineates the analytical and translational priorities most likely to advance mechanism-based therapeutic strategies.

bioinfo.title: Mechanistic gene-regulation-based trajectory inference with bowside
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract While single-cell RNA sequencing enables the in-depth study of differentiation processes, simultaneous trajectory inference and gene regulatory network reconstruction remain challenging. We propose bowside, a shallow neural stochastic differentiation model that mechanistically models gene regulation. Our method successfully recovers gene expression trends and the underlying regulatory interactions. We demonstrate bowside on hematopoiesis and induced pluripotent stem cell reprogramming data, retrieving known fate-determining network motifs.

bioinfo.title: Optimal transport reveals unresolved cells in single-cell multi-omics
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Single-cell multi-omics methods align cells across modalities, integrate them into one embedding and transfer labels between them. All three steps depend on a match between cells in two modalities, but this match usually stays hidden inside each tool. Its errors are hidden too, and every cell looks equally certain. Here we make the match explicit. For each pair of datasets, we build a soft coupling matrix with optimal transport and use it in three ways beyond estimating the match itself: to score how uncertain each cell’s match is, to upgrade existing integration and label-transfer tools without retraining them, and to decide which cells to set aside. Across 78 dataset pairs spanning six modality combinations, we evaluated ten integration and ten label-transfer tools using matched random removal as the control. We developed an ensemble coupling achieving the most accurate recovery of true cell pairs. Feeding couplings back into the tools improved label transfer clearly but improved integration only in how well the modalities mix. The ambiguity score, which we computed as a group-vote margin, gave the larger and more consistent gain in both tasks. Ambiguous-flagged cells matched worse in almost every dataset and removing them beat random removal in 98% of integration tests and 91% of label-transfer comparisons. These hard-to-integrate cells are mostly among rare, transitional and poorly measured populations. Making correspondence explicit therefore provides a practical way to distinguish reliable cross-modality results from uncertain ones while flagging cells that might have important roles in development and disease.

bioinfo.title: CellVADIS: Inferring cross-tissue immune cell trafficking dynamics from single-cell snapshots
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract The ability of immune cells to traffic between and enter different tissues is an important hallmark for effective immune responses. However, despite advances in high-throughput single-cell profiling, identifying circulating cell populations that drive tissue-specific immunity remains elusive. Here we present CellVADIS, an optimal transport based computational framework to infer cross-tissue immune cell dynamics. By connecting single-cell measurements across tissue sites, CellVADIS enables the prediction of cell migration fates, characterization of tissue-specific trafficking signatures on circulating cells, as well as identification of tissue entry points. We benchmarked our method against synthetic data and applied CellVADIS to two cross-tissue single-cell datasets which revealed characteristic marker expression patterns that define tissue-specific trafficking signatures and ‘homing’ niches of tissue-entering CD4 + and CD8 + T cells. CellVADIS provides a flexible, open-source tool for identifying cross-tissue single-cell dynamics from various high-throughput single-cell measurements, which would support the design of vaccination and immunotherapeutic regimens to generate tissue-specific immunity.

bioinfo.title: Single-cell multi-omics identify OTP and NOVA1 as regulators of leptin action in hypothalamic feeding circuits.
bioinfo.abstract: Leptin acts directly and indirectly on multiple neuronal populations to regulate feeding and numerous other physiologic functions. However, our understanding of how a single circulating signal coordinates diverse neuronal populations across multiple circuits is limited. To further elucidate how leptin reshapes molecular states in its direct and indirect neural targets, we combined time-resolved single-nucleus transcriptomics and chromatin accessibility profiling to map leptin-induced transcriptional and chromatin state changes across individual neurons in two key hypothalamic nuclei: the arcuate nucleus (ARC), which contains the majority of leptin receptor (LepR) neurons, and the paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus (PVH), an established downstream target of ARC LepR neurons. We found that leptin treatment of leptin-deficient ob/ob mice does not alter neuronal identity, but instead induces coordinated, cell-type-specific transcriptional and regulatory state changes that propagate hierarchically from the ARC to downstream PVH neurons. Integrating RNA velocity, cis-regulatory analysis, and cell-cell communication inference revealed that leptin modulates hypothalamic circuit architecture by selectively strengthening specific interactions while pruning broadly distributed, low-specificity signaling. Although leptin broadly activated STAT3 signaling across LepR neuronal subtypes, integrated multi-omic analyses revealed that activation of STAT3 engages distinct downstream regulatory programs in different neuronal populations, often with opposing physiological functions. Functional analyses identified the homeobox transcription factor OTP, a leptin-responsive regulator selectively induced in AGRP neurons, as a critical mediator of leptin-mediated inhibition of hunger-promoting AGRP neuronal activity and feeding. In parallel, unbiased analysis of PVH neuronal state transitions shows that NOVA1, an RNA-binding protein primarily expressed in inhibitory neurons, is regulated by leptin and alterations of NOVA1 expression bidirectionally control food intake and body weight. Together, these findings define a multi-layered regulatory framework through which leptin regulates hypothalamic feeding circuits to control energy balance.

bioinfo.title: A Multi-modal LLM-Knowledge Fusion Framework for Predicting Single-cell Genetic Perturbation Effects
bioinfo.abstract: Understanding cellular responses to genetic perturbations is fundamental for drug discovery, yet experimental approaches face significant limitations in coverage and cost that prevent comprehensive mapping of cellular behavior. This has motivated the development of virtual cells—computational models that learn the relationship between cell state and function to predict the consequences of perturbations across diverse contexts. However, current computational methods suffer from limited accuracy in complex genetic interactions, poor biological interpretability, and inadequate generalization to unseen genes, severely constraining virtual cell capabilities. We present scPert, a multi-modal framework based on Transformer architecture that integrates large language model embeddings with structured biological knowledge to predict single-cell transcriptomic responses to genetic perturbations. Through hierarchical fusion of knowledge graph representations, contextual embeddings from foundation models, and gene-specific encodings, scPert achieves significant performance improvements in both single-gene and combinatorial perturbations over existing methods. In cancer-relevant applications, scPert demonstrates the capability to reveal p53 pathway dynamics and immune checkpoint regulatory mechanisms. Systematic evaluation on 42 cancer dependency genes demonstrates scPert’s ability to identify critical potential therapeutic targets. Our framework establishes a powerful computational foundation for virtual cell construction and accelerates drug target discovery.

bioinfo.title: An interpretable Graph-Regularized Optimal Transport Framework for Diagonal Single-Cell Integrative Analysis
bioinfo.abstract: BACKGROUND: Recent advancements in single-cell omics technologies have enabled detailed characterization of cellular processes. However, coassay sequencing technologies remain limited, resulting in unpaired single-cell omics datasets with differing feature dimensions. FINDING: We present GROTIA (Graph-Regularized Optimal Transport Framework for Diagonal Single-Cell Integrative Analysis), a computational method to align multi-omics datasets without requiring any prior correspondence information. GROTIA achieves global alignment through optimal transport while preserving local relationships via graph regularization. Additionally, our approach provides interpretability by deriving domain-specific feature importance from partial derivatives, highlighting key biological markers. Moreover, the transport plan between modalities can be leveraged for post-integration clustering, enabling a data-driven approach to discover novel cell subpopulations. CONCLUSIONS: We demonstrate GROTIA's superior performance on four simulated and four real-world datasets, surpassing state-of-the-art unsupervised alignment methods and confirming the biological significance of the top features identified in each domain.

bioinfo.title: Chronic metabolic stress drives developmental programs and loss of tissue functions in non-transformed liver that mirror tumor states and stratify survival
bioinfo.abstract: Under chronic stress, cells must balance competing demands between cellular survival and tissue function. In metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD, formerly NAFLD/NASH), hepatocytes cooperate with structural and immune cells to perform crucial metabolic, synthetic, and detoxification functions despite nutrient imbalances. While prior work has emphasized stress-induced drivers of cell death, the dynamic adaptations of surviving cells and their functional repercussions remain unclear. Namely, we do not know which pathways and programs define cellular responses, what regulatory factors mediate (mal)adaptations, and how this aberrant activity connects to tissue-scale dysfunction and long-term disease outcomes. Here, by applying longitudinal single-cell multi-omics to a mouse model of chronic metabolic stress and extending to human cohorts, we show that stress drives survival-linked tradeoffs and metabolic rewiring, manifesting as shifts towards development-associated states in non-transformed hepatocytes with accompanying decreases in their professional functionality. Diet-induced adaptations occur significantly prior to tumorigenesis but parallel tumorigenesis-induced phenotypes and predict worsened human cancer survival. Through the development of a multi-omic computational gene regulatory inference framework and human in vitro and mouse in vivo genetic perturbations, we validate transcriptional (RELB, SOX4) and metabolic (HMGCS2) mediators that co-regulate and couple the balance between developmental state and hepatocyte functional identity programming. Our work defines cellular features of liver adaptation to chronic stress as well as their links to long-term disease outcomes and cancer hallmarks, unifying diverse axes of cellular dysfunction around core causal mechanisms.

bioinfo.title: Identification of gene kinetics patterns improves RNA velocity and cell fate prediction using JuloVelo
bioinfo.abstract: Single-cell RNA velocity has transformed our capacity to predict future cell states from sequencing snapshots, but existing methods rely on constant or binary kinetic assumptions that fail to capture the heterogeneous splicing dynamics of cellular differentiation. Here we present JuloVelo, a deep learning framework that demonstrates that identifying gene kinetics patterns to initialize neural network training dramatically improves RNA velocity model performance. By pre-determining whether each gene follows a Circle, Complete induction, or Complete repression pattern across cellular differentiation, JuloVelo initializes training with pattern-matched, pre-trained network weights, effectively guiding the cell-specific kinetics optimization away from biologically implausible parameter regimes. Additionally, JuloVelo demonstrates that multiome datasets can also be processed and modeled by utilizing promoter chromatin accessibility to guide kinetics pre-determination, and integrates an in silico perturbation framework to simulate transcription factor modulation on cell fate. Validated across eight datasets spanning erythrogenesis, neurogenesis, and endocrinogenesis, JuloVelo consistently outperformed constant-rate and cell-specific models, resolving the entire five-lineage differentiation program in hippocampal neurogenesis. Multiome processing improved both intrinsic and extrinsic velocity stability, and JuloVelo reduced computational execution time by approximately 70% compared to cellDancer. JuloVelo is available as an open-source package at https://github.com/jhlabtw/JuloVelo.jl.

bioinfo.title: Genetic Perturbation Prediction Models Fail Out-of-Distribution: A Rigorous Benchmark and Systematic Evaluation
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Perturbation prediction models - which forecast transcriptional responses to gene inactivation - are increasingly proposed as in silico surrogates for genome-scale drug discovery screens. Yet, rigorous evaluation of whether these models genuinely generalize beyond their training distribution has been lacking. Existing benchmarks rely predominantly on random train-test splits, obscuring systematic failure modes that only emerge under realistic out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions. Here we introduce EL-PERTURB (Extrapolative Learning for PERTURBation Prediction), a benchmarking framework that stress-tests 20 perturbation prediction models spanning six architecture classes on both essential gene and genome-wide Perturb- seq screens, using a novel stratified OOD splitting strategy that partitions train and test sets into functionally distinct regions of transcriptional space. We find that model performance degrades substantially under OOD conditions, and that architectural complexity - including single-cell foundation model embeddings - confers no reliable advantage over well-tuned simpler baselines. EL-PERTURB establishes a rigorous benchmark for perturbation effect prediction across a gradient of generalization difficulty, providing a guide for building models that can genuinely serve as surrogates for wet-lab screening.

bioinfo.title: Deep Lineage: Single-cell lineage tracing and fate inference using deep learning.
bioinfo.abstract: Recent advances in single-cell RNA sequencing and lineage tracing techniques have provided valuable insights into the temporal changes in gene expression during development, tumor progression, and disease onset. However, there are few computational methods available to analyze this information to help understand multicellular dynamics. We introduce Deep Lineage, a deep-learning method for analyzing time-series single-cell RNA sequencing with matched lineage tracing data. Our method accurately predicts early cell fate biases and gene expression profiles at different time points within a clone, surpassing existing methods in fate prediction accuracy. We further validate our model using LineageSim, a fate-aware lineage simulator, demonstrating robustness to technical noise such as barcode dropout and clone misidentification. Additionally, we apply Deep Lineage to in silico perturbations in cellular reprogramming and hematopoiesis to identify key genes and pathways associated with cell fate determination and propose testable perturbation hypotheses for experimental follow-up.

bioinfo.title: scMultiPreDICT: A single-cell predictive framework with transcriptomic and epigenetic signatures
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Cellular responses to genetic perturbations depend on both transcriptional programs and the epigenetic landscape. While single-cell multiomics technologies enable simultaneous profiling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility, the relative contribution of each regulatory layer to gene expression remains unclear. Existing computational approaches focus on data integration and gene regulatory network inference but do not systematically compare the predictive performance of transcriptional versus epigenetic features on a gene-by-gene basis. We present scMultiPreDICT, a computational framework for comparative predictive modeling of gene expression using single-cell multiomics data. scMultiPreDICT benchmarks RNA-only, ATAC-only and multimodal feature sets across six machine learning models including regression, tree-based learning and deep learning using multiple biological datasets. We show that RNA-derived features generally provide strong predictive power, whereas chromatin accessibility alone yields a modest performance. Surprisingly, multimodal integration does not uniformly improve prediction accuracy; instead, its benefit is gene-specific and context-dependent. Feature importance analysis reveals that transcriptional features dominate for most genes, whereas chromatin accessibility contributes meaningfully for a subset of genes in specific cellular contexts. Overall, the results demonstrate that regulatory layers contribute differently to gene expression. scMultiPreDICT provides a systematic framework for identifying the relative contributions of transcriptional and epigenetic regulation across genes and cellular contexts, guiding the design of targeted perturbation studies and the prioritization of regulatory layers for therapeutic interventions. scMultiPreDICT is implemented in R and available at https://github.com/UzunLab/scMultiPreDICT/ .

bioinfo.title: OT-knn: a neighborhood-aware optimal transport framework for aligning spatial transcriptomics data
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression while preserving spatial context within tissues, enabling detailed characterization of tissue organization. As ST technologies advance, aligning datasets across tissue sections, individuals, platforms, and developmental stages has become increasingly important but remains challenging due to sparse expression, biological heterogeneity, and geometric distortions between slices. We introduce OT-knn, a method for ST alignment that integrates local neighborhood information within an optimal transport framework. Rather than relying solely on single-spot expression, OT-knn reconstructs each spot using its spatial k -nearest neighbors, capturing microenvironment context that is more robust to noise and variability. These representations are then used to derive probabilistic correspondences between slices. We evaluate OT-knn using simulated data with known ground-truth alignment and real datasets from multiple ST platforms, including human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex data (10x Genomics Visium), mouse brain aging data with both within-donor and cross-donor comparisons (MERFISH), a multi-stage axolotl brain dataset (Stereo-seq), and a cross-platform analysis using mouse embryo datasets profiled by Stereo-seq and seqFISH. Across these settings, OT-knn achieves accurate and robust alignment, particularly in the presence of spatial deformation, donor heterogeneity, developmental variation and technological differences. Author summary Understanding how cells are arranged within tissues is important for studying how organs develop, age, and respond to disease. Spatial transcriptomics is a new technology that measures gene activity while keeping track of where each measurement comes from in the tissue. However, comparing data from different tissue slices, different individuals, or different time points is difficult. Tissues can change shape during preparation, gene measurements can be noisy, and natural biological differences exist across samples. In this work, we develop a method to better match corresponding regions across tissue slices. Instead of looking at each location by itself, we also consider information from its surrounding neighborhood. This provides a more stable and informative view of the tissue and makes it easier to match similar regions, even when the data are imperfect or the tissue shapes differ. We test our method on both simulated and real datasets from human, mouse, and axolotl brain tissues. Our approach enables more reliable comparisons of spatial gene activity across samples, which can help researchers study development, aging, and disease.

bioinfo.title: Identifiable inverse optimal transport for single-cell state transitions
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Signed effects of target-state programmes are unidentifiable in balanced optimal transport because fixed endpoint distributions make their contributions constant across feasible plans. We introduce UOT-IOT, a semi-relaxed inverse transport framework that restores measurable target-mass responses and provides a rank condition for local identifiability. It recovers coefficients in ground-truth benchmarks (correlation 0.997 versus 0.081 for balanced transport), transfers frozen directions to six unseen samples with specificity controls, and achieves the lowest transition error against seven methods under matched evaluation conditions. GH-IOT separates shared directions from context and lineage-history offsets, revealing opposing history-associated effects. IFN/HLA is associated with patient treatment response, whereas EMT relates to drug sensitivity and perturbation-induced state changes. PERSIST-IOT improves future population-composition prediction in an independent experiment. Together, these modules distinguish current state, transition propensity and future population outcomes while supporting testable biological interpretations.

bioinfo.title: A unified framework for defining and analyzing spatial niches in spatial omics data analysis
BioTrajX: evaluating biological plausibility in single-cell trajectory inference
bioinfo.abstract: Summary Trajectory inference (TI) methods reconstruct cellular progression from single-cell RNA sequencing data, typically by ordering cells along a pseudotime axis. However, different TI methods and analytical choices can produce divergent trajectories from the same dataset, making it difficult to determine which inferred trajectory best reflects the underlying biological process. Existing evaluation strategies often rely on computational benchmarks or qualitative biological assessment, with limited standardized approaches for incorporating a priori biological knowledge. Here, we present BioTrajX, an R package for biologically informed evaluation of pseudotime trajectories using three complementary metrics: Directionality (D), which measures agreement between pseudotime and expected biological progression; Order Consistency (O), which quantifies the coherence of marker-program changes along the trajectory; and Endpoint Validity (E), which assesses enrichment of expected cell states at trajectory endpoints. Together, the DOE metrics provide an interpretable framework for comparing alternative trajectory inference results and evaluating root-cell choices prior to downstream analyses. Availability and Implementation BioTrajX is implemented in R and freely available under the MIT License at https://github.com/irislity/BioTrajX . Code for reproducing the analyses and figures is available at https://github.com/irislity/BioTrajX_manuscript . Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

bioinfo.title: Efficient count-based models improve power and robustness for large-scale single-cell eQTL mapping
bioinfo.abstract: Population-scale single-cell RNA sequencing enables mapping genetic effects on gene regulation at the cellular level (for example, single-cell expression quantitative trait loci (sc-eQTLs)). However, existing sc-eQTL mapping approaches are either not designed for analyzing sparse counts in single-cell RNA sequencing data or become computationally intractable at scale. Here we developed jaxQTL—an efficient pseudobulk sc-eQTL mapping framework using highly efficient count-based models. In simulations, we demonstrated that jaxQTL with a negative binomial model provides calibrated inference while outperforming linear models. In OneK1K data, jaxQTL identified 16% more eGenes than linear models, while running substantially faster than single-cell Poisson mixed effect models. We found that fine-mapped sc-eQTLs are more distal from transcription starting site than those identified in all cells (bulk-eQTLs; P = 1 × 10 −4 ) and more enriched in cell-type-specific enhancers ( P = 3 × 10 −10 ), revealing distal regulatory effects that are missed in bulk tissues. Although sc-eQTLs are largely shared across cell types, cell-type-specificity increases with distance to transcription starting site. Finally, sc-eQTLs explain a greater proportion of single nucleotide polymorphism-heritability than bulk-eQTLs across 16 blood and immune-related traits (9.90 ± 0.88% versus 6.10 ± 0.76%) and prioritize disease-associated genes missed by the bulk approach (such as IL6ST ), improving, but not closing, the missing link between genome-wide association studies and eQTLs.

bioinfo.title: Single-cell transcriptomics in nutrition and metabolic research: Current approaches and emerging applications
bioinfo.abstract: Single-cell transcriptomics has emerged as a transformative approach for investigating cellular heterogeneity, nutrient-responsive signaling, and metabolic adaptation at unprecedented resolution. Unlike conventional bulk transcriptomics, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables characterization of cell-type-specific gene expression, dynamic cellular states, intercellular communication, and regulatory networks underlying nutrient metabolism in health and disease. Recent advances in scRNA-seq and complementary multi-omics technologies have expanded our understanding of how dietary factors and metabolic stress reshape cellular composition and function across key metabolic tissues, including the intestine, liver, adipose tissue, pancreas, skeletal muscle, and immune system. In this review, we summarize major methodological and computational approaches in single-cell transcriptomics, including sequencing platforms, trajectory inference, cell–cell communication analysis, gene regulatory network reconstruction, and integration with epigenomic, spatial transcriptomic, and metabolomic data. We then highlight emerging applications in nutrition and metabolic research, focusing on cellular heterogeneity in glucose and lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, nutrient sensing, inflammatory remodeling, and diet-responsive signaling. Particular attention is given to recent human studies revealing cell-type-specific responses to dietary interventions, caloric restriction, weight loss, and metabolic therapies. We also discuss key technical and analytical challenges, including sequencing depth, dropout events, batch effects, tissue dissociation artifacts, limited temporal resolution, and difficulties linking transcriptional states to dynamic metabolic flux. Although human applications remain relatively limited and are often constrained by small sample sizes and heterogeneous study designs, integration of scRNA-seq with spatial transcriptomics, single-cell multi-omics, metabolic profiling, and artificial intelligence-assisted analyses offers substantial opportunities to bridge molecular mechanisms with individual variation in nutritional responses. Collectively, these advances establish single-cell transcriptomics as a powerful framework for elucidating nutrient–cell interactions and advancing mechanistically informed precision nutrition.

bioinfo.title: scHGNN: A single-cell gene regulatory network inference method based on heuristic graph neural networks.
bioinfo.abstract: The construction of gene regulatory networks based on single-cell transcriptomics (scRNA-seq) data provides crucial technical support for decoding cell fate determination mechanisms at the single-cell level, elucidating molecular mechanisms underlying disease progression, and developing targeted therapeutics. Existing methods for constructing GRNs often rely excessively on gene expression features, struggling to achieve an effective balance between local direct regulatory signals and global multi-step regulatory pathways. This imbalance results in insufficient utilization of topological information within the network structure. Therefore, this study proposes a heuristic graph neural network-based GRN inference model (scHGNN). scHGNN integrates multi-order neighbor topological information into learnable weights through unified heuristic matrix and link prediction modules, thereby balancing local and global regulatory relationships. This approach effectively fuses gene expression features with network structural information to achieve precise inference of latent regulatory links within gene regulatory networks. Across GRN inference tasks using benchmark networks of varying gene scales and diverse origins, scHGNN consistently outperforms existing mainstream methods on key evaluation metrics. Furthermore, in target gene prediction cases for key transcription factors such as TP53, OTX2, and FOXP1, the model achieved validation rates as high as 76%-84% in the hTFtarget database. This not only supports its accuracy in identifying known regulatory relationships but also indicates its potential to identify high-confidence candidate regulatory interactions for further biological investigation. Collectively, these results demonstrate that scHGNN holds significant application value in elucidating gene regulatory mechanisms and exploring the molecular basis of related diseases.

bioinfo.title: Artificial Intelligence and Multi-Omics Integration for Predicting Stem Cell Fate A Conceptual Framework
bioinfo.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and high-throughput sequencing technologies have transformed stem cell research by enabling comprehensive characterization of cellular states at single-cell resolution. Despite these developments, integrating heterogeneous multi-omics datasets into predictive models of cell fate remains a major challenge. This article proposes a conceptual framework in which artificial intelligence serves as an integrative computational layer linking genomic, epigenomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and microenvironmental information. Within this framework, stem cell identity is represented as a dynamic multidimensional state, and AI models are used to infer trajectories, identify regulatory interactions, and generate experimentally testable hypotheses. The framework is intended to stimulate interdisciplinary research and does not claim validated predictive performance. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Stem Cells; Multi-Omics; Machine Learning; Systems Biology; Cell Fate Prediction; Computational Biology

bioinfo.title: Integrated metabolomic and single-cell analyses reveal crotonylation-related epithelial remodeling and SDC4 dysregulation in adenomyosis.
bioinfo.abstract: Adenomyosis (AM) is characterized by ectopic endometrial invasion and myometrial fibrosis, yet the molecular links between local metabolic remodeling, lysine crotonylation (Kcr), and epithelial dysfunction remain poorly understood. We investigated the metabolic and crotonylation-related landscape of AM and sought to identify epithelial molecular features associated with these alterations. Clinical metabolic profiles, public and newly generated tissue metabolomic data, crotonyl-CoA measurements, and tissue crotonylation assays were integrated with single-cell and bulk transcriptomic analyses. Kcr-related transcriptional patterns were characterized using multiple gene-set scoring approaches and co-expression analysis, followed by multi-algorithm feature prioritization. SDC4-associated epithelial states were further examined using trajectory inference, cell-cell communication analysis, transcription-factor prediction, and in silico perturbation. Adjusted clinical analyses showed no robust differences in circulating lipid profiles, whereas tissue-level metabolomic analyses revealed alterations in lipid- and lysine-related metabolites in AM. Crotonyl-CoA estimates were higher in AM tissue, accompanied by increased H3K18cr. A higher p65-associated Kcr signal was also observed in a single IP comparison; given that only one IP measurement was available per group, this finding should be considered a preliminary descriptive observation. Single-cell analyses identified prominent Kcr-related transcriptional patterns in epithelial cells and linked this state to adhesion, junctional organization, and epithelial remodeling. SDC4 was consistently prioritized across five machine-learning procedures and was predominantly expressed in epithelial populations. SDC4-positive epithelial cells exhibited distinct inferred differentiation states and intercellular communication patterns, while computational perturbation further implicated SDC4-associated networks in epithelial adhesion, cytoskeletal organization, and junctional regulation. These findings connect local metabolic remodeling and crotonylation-related alterations with a distinct epithelial transcriptional state in AM and identify SDC4 as a consistently prioritized candidate associated with epithelial remodeling. The preliminary p65-associated Kcr observation provides additional context for investigating potential associations among Kcr, p65, and SDC4-related epithelial programs.

bioinfo.title: Fundamental errors in RNA velocity arising from the omission of cell growth
bioinfo.abstract: The ultimate promise of single cell "RNA velocity" methods is compelling: in principle, one can project forward the transcriptional state of each cell and map long-term expression trajectories. While there has been robust and ongoing articulation of limitations of existing methods, consensus frameworks fail to account for a fundamental aspect of cellular dynamics: growth. In a growing population, biomass (including RNA and other macromolecules) is constantly accumulating. This implies a homeostatic velocity (defined in the terms of production and degradation) that is positive, which is at odds with the conventional estimation, interpretation, and uses of velocity. Here, we investigate the consequences of omitting cell growth from the RNA velocity framework. We demonstrate systematic errors that arise in simulations of growing cells and show evidence for these artifacts in existing data. Finally, we point the way forward and highlight that explicitly accounting for cell growth can lead to new biological insights.

bioinfo.title: Large language models complement established workflows for mechanistic model construction and refinement in systems biology
bioinfo.abstract: Mechanistic models provide a framework for describing, understanding, and predicting biological processes, but their development requires an interdisciplinary team with expertise in biology, mathematics, and computation. Here we present Octomod, a multi-agent workflow based on large language models (LLMs) that integrates biological knowledge retrieval, model construction, parameter estimation, and hypothesis testing. Built on established software tools, including AMICI and pyPESTO, and community standards, including SBML and PEtab, Octomod supports model development and refinement through natural-language interaction with a user. The agents' proposals must pass defined checks and the user's decision before they are used. Every input, model, check, and decision is recorded, so that model building remains transparent and reproducible. We applied Octomod to four problems. Three used published data and differ in model size and in how much the user guided the run: Octomod constructed a model that matched a published model without user guidance, supported the interactive refinement of a gene-regulatory model, and built models of cell-cell communication that explained the responses of five immune cell types to different stimuli. In the fourth application, on newly generated and unpublished lipidomics data, Octomod helped to determine which processes the measurements could inform, identify unresolved label fluxes, and reduce a supplied model to those processes. Together, these results show how LLMs can strengthen and complement established workflows for constructing and refining biologically informed models.

bioinfo.title: Inferring gene regulatory networks from single-cell perturbation data by optimizing causal reach of latent mediator dynamics.
bioinfo.abstract: Resolving the causal structure of gene regulatory networks is central to understanding cellular regulation. Pooled CRISPR screens with single-cell RNA readouts measure the transcriptional consequences of many interventions in parallel, providing a powerful resource for causal discovery. Combinatorial designs that perturb multiple regulators per cell increase throughput and can reveal responses that single-gene perturbations do not. However, inferring causal gene networks from these experiments remains challenging because gene regulatory interactions are nonlinear, dynamic, and often involve feedback. Thus, attributing the combined effect of several perturbations to individual regulators remains difficult. Additionally, transcriptional regulation is ultimately carried out by proteins, while single-cell perturbation datasets generally measure only RNA levels. Existing methods often simplify regulatory dynamics or rely on assumptions that conflict with gene regulation, such as acyclicity. Moreover, current evaluation practices usually rely on expression prediction error, which is readily computable in real datasets, but does not necessarily reflect graph quality. A complementary metric is needed to assess inferred regulatory connections using observed perturbation responses in real data. To address these challenges, we present CausalODE, a differentiable framework for learning causal graphs from single-cell perturbation data. Our approach incorporates three central insights to improve upon previous methods. First, genes that are differentially expressed when a gene is perturbed should be downstream of the target gene in the regulatory network; we quantify this property with a metric we term causal reach. Second, causal interactions involve transient cellular responses in RNA transcription, splicing, and degradation. Third, gene regulatory interactions are mediated by proteins, whose levels are not directly measured in single-cell RNA-seq experiments. Building on these insights, CausalODE learns a graph that optimizes the causal reach metric, captures transient cellular responses to perturbation, and explicitly models the latent dynamics of protein levels. Together, these components allow nonlinear responses, feedback loops, and time-lagged regulation. Across simulated Perturb-seq datasets with different sparsities and graph structures, CausalODE improves AUPRC and precision among top-ranked edges compared with baselines and competing methods, while achieving competitive AUROC. We introduce a metric to evaluate the causal reach of inferred graphs on real data by measuring how well the graphs explain differentially expressed genes in single-cell perturbation experiments. Using this metric, CausalODE outperforms the strongest competing method or baseline by approximately 60% on the CaRPool-seq knockdown dataset and 80% on the Norman et al. activation dataset. Its top-ranked edges generally show greater enrichment for high-confidence evidence from cell-type-matched ChIP-seq, CollecTRI, and regulatory STRING than those of other methods. The inferred graphs also distin-guish non-additive from approximately additive genetic interactions in held-out perturbation pairs. Finally, ablation analyses show that optimizing causal reach improves performance on held-out perturbations, and the learned latent regulator activities track simulated protein dynamics, with median temporal correlations ranging from 0.79 to 0.99.
