bioinfo.title: Nonreciprocal Hopfield nets for angiogenesis.
bioinfo.abstract: During sprouting angiogenesis, endothelial cells dynamically reorganize among three relevant phenotypes (glycolytic, stalk and tip) to form new blood vessels, with cells transitioning from one phenotype to another. These cell-state transitions may involve intrinsic nonequilibrium dynamics that go beyond relaxation of the conventional Waddington landscape. We investigate this possibility using a nonreciprocal Hopfield network inferred from single-cell RNA sequencing and RNA velocity data for 1896 endothelial cells on a panel of 1873 genes. We encode the three experimentally identified phenotypes as correlated memory patterns and introduce an asymmetric mixing matrix describing their effective interactions. A dynamical mean- field reduction yields a three-dimensional system for the overlaps with these phenotypic memories, whose parameters are fitted to RNA-velocity-derived trajectories. The nonreciprocal model outperforms its reciprocal counterpart on held-out testing data. Remarkably, its long-time dynamics exhibit either stationary attractors or sustained cycles connecting phenotypic states, depending on the inference timescale. These results suggest that angiogenic cell fate decisions may involve directed, non-relaxational dynamics that cannot be captured by a conventional energy landscape. This approach may also provide a useful framework for investigating how perturbations constrain cellular differentiation.

bioinfo.title: scCody distinguishes aging-aligned from divergent disease-associated cellular remodeling
bioinfo.abstract: Biological aging clocks summarize molecular changes as a single age estimate, but cannot distinguish disease-associated changes that follow healthy aging from those that deviate from it. Here we introduce scCody, a generative framework that learns age-dependent cellular population dynamics from cross-sectional single-cell cohorts using population-level optimal transport and endpoint-consistency regularization. scCody accurately reconstructed cellular populations at unseen ages, recovered age-associated transcriptional changes more effectively than existing generative dynamics models, and enabled donor-age inference without direct age-regression training. Using the learned healthy aging reference, scCody decomposed disease-associated cellular displacement into aging-aligned and orthogonal components. In Alzheimer's disease, selected neuronal populations showed substantial aging-aligned remodeling alongside shared orthogonal changes associated with established pathology signatures. In contrast, COVID-19 exhibited weaker aging alignment and more pronounced orthogonal immune remodeling. Further decomposition revealed patient-level interferon variation associated with symptom duration and increased transcriptional heterogeneity in CD16 monocytes. This framework provides an extension of biological age assessment beyond a single age estimate, distinguishing cellular changes that resemble healthy aging from those that depart from it.

bioinfo.title: Predicting cell fate via intelligent porous microcapsules: A multiphysics computational design framework
bioinfo.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Controlled and localized release of biochemical signals is essential for regulating cell differentiation, proliferation, apoptosis, and migration during tissue regeneration. Uncontrolled release can cause adverse effects such as inflammation or fibrotic tissue formation, whereas gradual and spatially confined delivery enables precise modulation of cell behavior. Microcapsule-based systems represent a promising strategy to engineer these interactions. In this study, a multiphysics computational design framework is developed to model the coupled mechanisms of molecular diffusion and fundamental cellular processes within extracellular matrices containing porous microcapsules. METHODS: Molecular release is described using Fick's law, with the membrane modeled as a porous barrier with an effective diffusivity dependent on porosity and thickness. Cell motility is governed by a force-balance formulation, while proliferation and differentiation are regulated by cell deformation and a maturation threshold time dependent on integrated mechanical and chemical stimuli. The model was implemented in a standardized COMSOL and Abaqus environment and validated against Lattice Boltzmann reference data. RESULTS: The model showed excellent agreement with reference data for numerical verification of the transport solver. Parametric analyses indicate that increasing membrane porosity accelerates transport, while thickness acts as a resistive barrier. An empirical design equation was derived to act as a computational surrogate, enabling the a priori selection of structural parameters to match specific tissue maturation windows without experimental trial-and-error. Simulations demonstrate that centrally positioned microcapsules generate synergistic chemical-mechanical cues that maximize the cellular response (15 cells) compared to peripheral configurations. CONCLUSION: The proposed framework provides a predictive computational design tool for the rational design of microstructured delivery systems to optimize tissue regeneration.

bioinfo.title: multiVIB: A unified probabilistic contrastive learning framework for atlas-scale integration of single-cell multi-omics data
PROFET predicts continuous gene expression dynamics from scRNA-seq data to elucidate heterogeneity of cancer treatment responses.
bioinfo.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) profiles cellular heterogeneity but captures only static snapshots, limiting inference of gene expression dynamics. We developed PROFET (particle-based reconstruction of generative force-matched expression trajectories), a framework that reconstructs continuous, nonlinear single-cell trajectories from sparsely sampled scRNA-seq time series. PROFET combines a particle-based gradient-flow algorithm with simulation-free force matching to accurately infer cellular dynamics. Across mouse and human in vitro datasets and an in vivo axolotl regeneration dataset, PROFET achieved 2.6-12.5× lower prediction error than ten state-of-the-art trajectory inference methods. Applying PROFET to newly generated scRNA-seq data from a palbociclib-treated MCF7 cell line and three published breast cancer patient datasets, we reconstructed treatment-response trajectories and identified a resistant cell subpopulation exhibiting large phenotypic shifts and enrichment of the surface markers UNC5B, TLR3, PCDH19, PROCR, SLITRK6, and SEMA6B. PROFET provides a biologically grounded framework for reconstructing cell-state dynamics from static single-cell data across development, regeneration, and therapeutic response. A record of this paper's transparent peer review process is included in the supplemental information.

bioinfo.title: Context-Aware Protein Representations Using Protein Language Models and Optimal Transport
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Proteins have different functions in different contexts. As a result, representations that take into account a protein’s biological context would allow for a more accurate assessment of its functions and properties. Protein language models (PLMs) generate amino-acid-level (residue-level) embeddings of proteins and are a powerful approach for creating universal protein representations. However, PLMs on their own do not consider context and cannot generate context-specific protein representations. We introduce COPTER, a method that uses optimal transport to pool together a protein’s PLM-generated residue-level embeddings using a separate context embedding to create context-aware protein representations. We conceptualize the residue-level embeddings as samples from a probabilistic distribution, and use sliced Wasserstein distances to map these samples against a context-specific reference set, yielding a contextualized protein-level embedding. We evaluate COPTER’s performance on three downstream prediction tasks: therapeutic drug target prediction, genetic perturbation response prediction, and TCR-epitope binding prediction. Compared to state-of-the-art baselines, COPTER achieves substantially improved, near-perfect performance in predicting therapeutic targets across cell contexts. It also results in improved performance in predicting responses to genetic perturbations and binding between TCRs and epitopes. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/SahilP113/COPTER .

bioinfo.title: Network inference at single-cell resolution reveals morphoregulatory divergence and multilayered buffering in limb evolution.
bioinfo.abstract: How changes in conserved developmental genetic programs contribute to morphological evolution remains poorly understood, particularly in non-conventional model species. Here, we combine single-cell transcriptomic and chromatin-accessibility profiling with cross-species label transfer and gene regulatory network inference to compare mouse and pig limb development. Our analyses identify broadly conserved cellular organization but discrete divergence in HOX-, FGF- and SHH-regulated programs. FGFR inhibition in mouse limb buds phenocopies the distal expansion of pig GREM1 expression, while altered SHH responses and anterior-posterior polarity converge on the PTCH1 regulatory landscape. Its functional dissection reveals degeneration of a limb regulatory module in artiodactyls, conservation of an additional distal enhancer, and extensive redundancy among cis-regulatory inputs. Allele-specific analyses further show that reduced Ptch1 dosage is buffered by transcriptional compensation. Together, these findings reveal how cis-regulatory and pathway-level robustness can accommodate distributed regulatory change while preserving developmental function, providing a mechanistic framework for the evolution of artiodactyl limb morphology.

bioinfo.title: Graph-guided flow matching enables biologically informed prediction at single-cell resolution
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Perturb-seq enables systematic interrogation of massively parallel genetic perturbations at single-cell resolution, yet exhaustive characterization of the full perturbation space remains impractical. Here, we present Graph-guided Flow Matching (GFM), a generative framework that integrates biological knowledge graphs with latent flow matching to predict post-perturbation single-cell transcriptomes. Across multiple large-scale Perturb-seq datasets, GFM outperforms a strong linear baseline and current deep-learning models in predicting unseen single-gene perturbations, while training up to 30x faster and remaining robust with limited training data. GFM also demonstrates competitive performance in the two-gene perturbation prediction task when neither perturbed gene is observed during training. Ablation experiments show that combining flow matching with knowledge graphs enables accurate prediction of perturbation responses. Finally, GFM accurately calculates transcriptional consequences of HSP90AA1 inactivation and identifies target candidates unseen by the model in chronic myeloid leukemia. Our study establishes GFM as a biologically informed generative framework that predicts single-cell perturbation responses for prioritization of therapeutic targets.

bioinfo.title: SPARK: Bayesian Structure Learning of Enhancer-based Gene Regulatory Networks from Single-cell Multiomics Data and Prior Knowledge
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Enhancer-based gene regulatory networks (eGRNs) linking enhancers with recruited transcription factors (TFs) and downstream target genes can help decipher complex regulatory mechanisms, such as the function of GWAS variants at enhancers. Molecular assays that profile gene expression and chromatin state jointly from the same cells (such as 10x Multiome) are a rich source of input data for eGRN reconstruction. However, these assays lack mechanistic evidence for enhancer-gene and TF-enhancer links, which can be contributed by prior knowledge from other assays and analyses. Here, we present SPARK, an eGRN reconstruction framework that formally combines single-cell multiome data with mechanistic prior knowledge. SPARK represents eGRNs as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and learns them using Bayesian inference, with a prior on the network structure constructed from heterogeneous sources of evidence. In a simulation study, we show that SPARK benefits from prior knowledge and outperforms existing DAG-based and regression-based algorithms. Finally, we use SPARK to study the regulatory circuitry of enhancers harboring immune disease GWAS variants in human primary monocytes, revealing known and novel regulatory links as candidates for experimental validation.

bioinfo.title: bulk2scDiff: A Pseudobulk-Conditioned Diffusion Model for Bulk-to-Single-Cell RNA-Seq Generation
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Bulk RNA sequencing remains the predominant profiling strategy for large clinical cohorts, but it aggregates transcriptional signals across cell populations, thereby masking the underlying cellular heterogeneity. Inferring this heterogeneity from existing bulk transcriptomic data could extend large cohort-based studies that have already been profiled, but constitutes an underdetermined inverse problem, as one bulk profile can be compatible with multiple underlying cellular populations. Existing computational deconvolution methods address this problem primarily by estimating cell-type proportions or cell-type-averaged expression profiles rather than resolving expression at the level of individual cells. Here, we present bulk2scDiff, a proof-of-concept conditional diffusion framework that reformulates bulk-to-single-cell inference as conditional generation of single-cell expression profiles from pseudobulk transcriptomic input. We evaluated bulk2scDiff on two cancer single-cell RNA sequencing datasets, breast cancer and acute myeloid leukemia, where pseudobulk profiles were derived from the single-cell data and used as conditioning inputs, with the matched single-cell populations providing ground truth for controlled evaluation. Across both cases, bulk2scDiff closely reconstructed populations from training samples and generated biologically coherent single-cell populations for held-out samples, generalizing most consistently to recurrent immune features. A pseudobulk-swap control further confirmed sample-specific conditioning, with each sample’s corresponding pseudobulk yielding the closest agreement with its observed population in nearly all cases. Overall, our work establishes the feasibility of conditional diffusion for generating single-cell populations from pseudobulk transcriptomic profiles, providing a foundation for future evaluation with clinical bulk RNA sequencing data.

bioinfo.title: S100A11 sustains STRAP stability to drive PI3K/AKT/NF-κB feedforward signalling circuit activation in colorectal cancer progression.
bioinfo.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains one of the most prevalent malignancies worldwide, with persistently low rates of early-stage diagnosis, poor overall prognosis, and a propensity for therapeutic resistance-challenges that underscore the urgent need for deeper mechanistic insight. By integrating single-cell transcriptomic data (GSE161277) with multi-omics datasets from TCGA and GEO repositories, alongside an independent clinical cohort, we identified S100A11 as a consistently overexpressed gene in CRC that correlates significantly with adverse patient outcomes. Functional studies established that S100A11 drives tumour progression by promoting cell proliferation, suppressing apoptosis, and inducing epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Mechanistically, S100A11 engages the WD6-7 domain (residues 221-302) of STRAP through direct physical interaction, thereby recruiting the deubiquitylase OTUB1 to shield lysine K246 of STRAP from K63-linked polyubiquitination. This protection stabilises STRAP and facilitates its association with PI3K, culminating in activation of the PI3K/AKT/NF-κB cascade and nuclear translocation of p65. We further demonstrate that p65 binds directly to the promoter regions of both S100A11 and STRAP, transcriptionally upregulating their expression and establishing a self-reinforcing feedforward loop that sustains pathway activation. Collectively, these findings delineate a hierarchical regulatory network centred on the S100A11/STRAP/NF-κB axis and offer a mechanistic framework with potential implications for CRC diagnosis and targeted intervention.

bioinfo.title: VCBench: A Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Single-Cell Foundation Models
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Single-cell foundation models are increasingly positioned as virtual cells, yet their capabilities are assessed by fragmented, largely single-task benchmarks that obscure where these models improve on simple baselines. VCBench addresses this by synthesizing four independent virtual-cell frameworks into seven capability dimensions: perturbation response prediction, cross-species universality, gene regulatory network (GRN) inference, modality integration, temporal dynamics, multi-scale integration, and in silico experimentation. Each dimension is assessed for operational testability under current architectures and datasets: five admit direct or proxy evaluation, while multi-scale integration and in silico experimentation are structurally untestable as end-to-end tasks. We evaluate five foundation models (Geneformer, scGPT, UCE, TranscriptFormer, Arc State) against pre-registered linear and nearest-neighbor baselines across the five testable dimensions, and report three findings. First, the baselines match or exceed every foundation model on four of the five scored dimensions, replicating the reported competitiveness of linear baselines on perturbation prediction and extending it to cross-species transfer, GRN inference, and temporal ordering. Second, TranscriptFormer alone exceeds the strongest baseline on cross-modal RNA-to-protein prediction (53% Pearson improvement, with a documented contamination caveat) and is the only model to reach Level 2 in the pre-registered Virtual Cell (VC) Level rubric; the architectural choice behind this advantage simultaneously causes a spectral collapse that destroys its temporal-ordering performance, a tradeoff invisible to single-task benchmarks. Third, no foundation model publishes a complete cell-level training manifest, leaving data contamination undetectable to users. Alongside the benchmark, VCBench releases a Contamination Reporting Schema and contributes two further methodological tools: a common-label-set protocol that controls for class-count confounds in cross-species transfer, and a spread-error correlation probe for epistemic calibration.

bioinfo.title: Adaptive Framework for Integrating Regulatory Pathways and Cellular Signaling in Single Cell Biology
bioinfo.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has transformed the study of cellular heterogeneity, enabling detailed characterization of cell types, regulatory programs, and disease-associated transcriptional changes. However, the growing number of computational methods for core analysis tasks introduces variability and limits reproducibility across datasets. In this dissertation, I present a generalizable computational framework for single-cell analysis that integrates regulatory pathways and cellular signaling to improve biological interpretability. First, I develop consensus-based methods for key scRNA-seq tasks, including cell clustering and gene regulatory network inference, leveraging a wisdom-of-crowds strategy to enhance performance across datasets. Second, I introduce novel approaches for cell-type-resolved marker gene selection and signaling-informed transcription factor activity estimation, incorporating both downstream gene expression and upstream cell–cell communication signals to better capture regulatory mechanisms. Finally, I apply state of the art single cell genomics analysis methods to disease contexts in neurology and cancer, using single-cell and spatial transcriptomics to uncover cell-type-specific signaling and transcriptional changes associated with disease progression and therapeutic response. Together, this work bridges methodological development and biomedical application, providing a unified framework for integrating cellular signaling and gene regulation in single-cell genomics.

bioinfo.title: CellPatch: a flexible and efficient framework for single-cell foundation models empowered by heuristic gene patching
bioinfo.abstract: Foundation models have advanced single-cell omics analysis but often remain too complex for practical use. We present CellPatch, a lightweight foundation model combining cross-attention with heuristic gene patching to reduce computational complexity during pretraining and fine-tuning while enabling inspection of gene-attention patterns. Across single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets spanning multiple organs and tissue states, CellPatch achieves state-of-the-art performance on diverse prediction tasks. Its modular design supports linear, adapter-based and task-specific architectures, enabling CellPatch to be adapted to diverse biological tasks.

bioinfo.title: scRep: A Latent-Space Self-Distilled Foundation Model for Single-Cell Representation Learning
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Single-cell foundation models have shown strong potential for learning transferable representations from large-scale transcriptomic data. However, many existing approaches rely on reconstructing masked gene expression values, creating a potential mismatch between observation-space reconstruction and the goal of learning stable biological representations. This challenge is particularly relevant to single-cell RNA sequencing, where sparsity, incomplete gene detection, and technical variation can obscure the underlying biological state. Here, we introduce scRep, a compact latent-space self-distillation framework for single-cell representation learning. Rather than reconstructing raw expression values, scRep aligns differently perturbed views of the same cell through a momentum-updated teacher–student architecture, with self-distillation objectives at both the cell and gene levels. This representation-centered formulation encourages the model to capture biological information that remains stable across incomplete and perturbed transcriptomic observations. Using frozen representations without task-specific fine-tuning, scRep pretrained on approximately 2.8 million cells achieves the strongest overall performance across the evaluated frozen-representation benchmarks, demonstrating strong sample efficiency. A larger-scale scRep model pretrained on 30.72 million cells further demonstrates that the framework remains effective when scaled to a substantially larger and more diverse corpus. Beyond cell identity, scRep prioritizes established marker genes, recovers transcription factor–associated gene programs with cell-type-specific activity, and preserves continuous developmental structure that supports graph-based pseudotime inference. We further show that pretraining performance is closely associated with biological diversity: reducing redundant cells while improving cell-type coverage can match or exceed the performance of larger, less balanced training corpora. Together, these results establish latent-space self-distillation as an effective alternative to expression reconstruction for single-cell foundation modeling and suggest that efficient scaling depends not only on the number of cells, but also on the learning objective and the biological diversity of the pretraining corpus.

bioinfo.title: Evaluation of a deep generative computational framework under constrained conditions for multi-regional placental single-cell transcriptomic inference
LongAllele: a joint inference framework for allele-specific analysis on long-read bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Allele-specific analysis from RNA-seq is a powerful approach to characterize cis -regulatory effects. However, existing methods remain limited in both haplotype inference and allelic testing. Their haplotype-inference workflows separate variant calling, haplotype phasing, and read-haplotype assignment into sequential steps, failing to fully exploit within-read single-nucleotide variant (SNV) linkage information and propagating errors into downstream allelic analysis. At the testing stage, they ignore non-phasable reads lacking heterozygous SNVs, biasing calls and inflating false positives, and remain incomplete across gene-, isoform-, and local-event-level variant effects. Here, we present LongAllele, a statistical framework that employs an expectation-maximization algorithm to jointly infer heterozygous variants, haplotype structure, and read-haplotype assignments from long-read bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing. LongAllele further introduces phasability-aware testing that explicitly accounts for non-phasable reads, avoiding inflated false-positive calls when haplotype information is incomplete. It also enables comprehensive allelic testing across gene-level allele-specific expression (ASE), isoform-level allele-specific transcript usage (ASTU), and local-event-level haplotype-associated exon and junction usage (HAEU and HAJU), providing a multi-scale view of cis -regulation across biological contexts. We applied LongAllele to long-read RNA-seq datasets spanning GTEx (multi-tissue bulk), peripheral blood mononuclear cells (single-cell), human hippocampus (single-nucleus), and human cortex from two Alzheimer’s disease (AD) case-control cohorts (bulk, Oxford Nanopore and PacBio). LongAllele consistently revealed greater context dependence in expression-level than isoform-level allelic regulation across tissues, cell types, and disease states, and pinpointed high-impact regulatory variants including rare splice-site mutations missed by standalone variant callers. It further showed that purifying selection constrains allelic imbalance at both gene and isoform levels and resolved AD-associated variant effects in individual transcriptomes across long-read platforms.

bioinfo.title: FastCCC: A permutation-free framework for scalable, robust, and reference-based cell-cell communication analysis in single cell transcriptomics studies
bioinfo.abstract: Detecting cell-cell communications (CCCs) in single-cell transcriptomics studies is fundamental for understanding the function of multicellular organisms. Here, we introduce FastCCC, a permutation-free framework that enables scalable, robust, and reference-based analysis for identifying critical CCCs and uncovering biological insights. FastCCC relies on fast Fourier transformation-based convolution to compute p-values analytically without permutations, introduces a modular algebraic operation framework to capture a broad spectrum of CCC patterns, and can leverage atlas-scale single cell references to enhance CCC analysis on user-collected datasets. To support routine reference-based CCC analysis, we constructed the first human CCC reference panel, encompassing 19 distinct tissue types, over 450 unique cell types, and approximately 16 million cells. We demonstrate the advantages of FastCCC across multiple datasets, most of which exceed the analytical capabilities of existing CCC methods. In real datasets, FastCCC reliably captures biologically meaningful CCCs, even in highly complex tissue environments, including differential interactions between endothelial and immune cells linked to COVID-19 severity, dynamic communications in thymic tissue during T-cell development, as well as distinct interactions in reference-based CCC analysis.

bioinfo.title: Calibrating developmental dynamics from single-cell atlases: lineage paths outrun least-action routes
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Single-cell atlases infer developmental dynamics from destructive snapshots, yet how far realized lineage paths depart from such inferred dynamics has never been measured with controls. We introduce LADD (Least-Action Developmental Dynamics), a measurement framework that learns a stochastic developmental vector field from time-series single-cell RNA-seq and computes minimum-action and minimum-time paths, together with a three-layer calibration protocol that separates genuine path deviation from the generic cost of centroid measurement, and we compare its forecasting component with optimal-transport and flow-matching methods. In the lineage-resolved Caenorhabditis elegans atlas, the raw action ratio of observed lineage-centroid trajectories to optimal paths is 3.79, yet forward-simulated ensembles of the learned model itself score 2.07, leaving a genuine excess of about two-fold. In zebrafish ( Danio rerio ), the observed ratio sits entirely at the model’s floor. Three mechanisms that could explain the residual deviation (detours, flow-opposition, and fate-map complexity) are each excluded; what remains is speed, with lineages moving 30–43% faster along the learned flow. We report validity boundaries for temporal resolution, cross-species comparison, and energetic interpretation, delimiting where action-based trajectory comparisons are meaningful. Author Summary Embryos develop from a single cell into many specialized cell types, and modern atlases let researchers watch this process as a movie of molecular snapshots. Because each cell is measured only once, software must stitch snapshots into “trajectories”, and some studies ask whether development follows optimal routes, such as paths of least action (a principle borrowed from physics). Here we provide LADD, a method that learns the dynamics of development from such atlases and computes the optimal paths those dynamics imply, together with a calibration protocol that distinguishes genuine biological deviation from artifacts created by measuring averages of cell populations. Applying it to worm and zebrafish embryogenesis, we find that most of the apparent deviation from optimality is such a measurement artifact; what remains in the worm is a modest, genuine excess arising because lineages move faster than the optimal route, not around it. LADD offers a reusable way to test optimality claims about development against an explicit noise floor.

bioinfo.title: Inference of cell division parameters in bacteria under transient growth conditions.
bioinfo.abstract: Most quantitative models of bacterial cell division assume steady-state growth, yet natural environments are highly dynamic. Here, we infer division control parameters of E. coli from single-cell size trajectories under nonsteady growth. We describe growth as a continuous process interrupted by stochastic divisions, whose propensity depends on cell size and on the size added since birth. Combining an estimation of time-dependent single-cell growth rates with a maximum-likelihood estimator that we previously validated on synthetic data, we obtain time-resolved estimates of the mean added size at division, its noise, and a strategy parameter that measures how added size depends on birth size. This parameter vanishes for the adder , in which cells add, on average, a fixed size regardless of their size at birth, and is negative for sizer-adder control, in which larger-born cells add less size. We apply this approach to published single-cell data covering steady exponential growth, gradual nutrient depletion, and exit from starvation. We implement a time-resolved model selection based on the Akaike information criterion, concluding that the adder is sufficient during steady growth, whereas size dynamics during entry into and exit from stationary phase are better explained by transient deviations toward sizer-adder control. The framework provides a general method to quantify time-resolved changes in the scale, stochasticity, and strategy of division in nonsteady environments.

bioinfo.title: SPECHTacle: An Efficient Detection and Visualization of Cell Specific Regulation in Single Cell-Based Experiments Using a Novel Combinatorial Computational Tool
bioinfo.abstract: ABSTRACT Herein, we describe SPECHTacle, a novel computational tool affording the ability to efficiently visualize and delineate the specific cellular population(s) impacted by an experimental paradigm utilizing heterogeneous cell-based samples. SPECHTacle can be employed to efficiently determine, in a cell specific manner, the populations preferentially impacted by treatments, drugs, injuries, disease states, and/or development within datasets continuously being generated across nearly countless subfields in molecular biology. SPECHTacle accomplishes this task by harnessing the power of Waddington optimal transport analysis and Shannon entropy in a combinatorial fashion to distinguish cell populations preferentially altered due to nearly any experimental paradigm and generates a visual representation of cellular entropy (i.e. change) across entire datasets. Ultimately, this allows for efficient determination of specific populations preferentially impacted by an experimental paradigm and identifies populations to target for downstream analyses employing quantitative measurements. We propose that SPECHTacle represents an immediately useful computational tool with the potential to be integrated into single cell-based workflows and greatly enhance the efficiency of both manual and machine-based learning workflows.

bioinfo.title: Building virtual cell dynamics that evolve with biological measurements
bioinfo.abstract: Virtual cell models built from single-cell measurements need to predict how cells change over time, but new biological measurements often reveal dynamical relationships that existing models cannot express. Translating such measurements into dynamics therefore requires deciding what biological relation should be modeled, where it should enter the formulation and how its recovery should be validated. Here we present CellCompass, an agentic AI system that couples a scientific agent with an extensible dynamical engine for modeling state transitions and population change, along with fate and molecular readout. CellCompass reuses existing formulations when sufficient and designs, implements and refines new ones when experimental measurements introduce additional constraints. To assess this capability, we developed DynBench100, a benchmark of 100 simulated single-cell time-course scenarios with hidden dynamical ground truth. CellCompass achieved the highest aggregate performance among the tested general-purpose and biomedical agents across six dynamical tasks. Across four real single-cell studies, it retained an existing velocity-growth model to reconstruct context-dependent epithelial-mesenchymal transition and developed three new dynamical formulations for distinct experimental measurements. In drug-response data, incorporating metabolic RNA labeling reduced pulse-control identifiability error by 31.1%, revealing staged response programs and generating testable predictions for perturbing a candidate adaptive program. In hematopoietic lineage tracing, incorporating clonal barcodes improved clone-fate agreement by 54% over the strongest dynamical baseline, identifying early lineage priming among transcriptionally similar progenitors. Finally, in time-resolved CITE-seq data, CellCompass reduced future surface-protein distribution error by 13.2% for RNA-initialized trajectories, uncovering lineage-specific temporal offsets between transcriptional and protein programs. Together, CellCompass provides a framework in which virtual-cell dynamics can expand with the biological measurements used to constrain them.

bioinfo.title: ComicGTN infers disease-associated rare cell states from single-cell multiomic data using DNA sequence–augmented graph transformer networks
bioinfo.abstract: Single-cell multiomic technology makes it possible to profile both the transcriptome and epigenome within individual cells. The detection of rare cell states from such data is crucial for exploring novel disease biomarkers with clinical potential. However, existing methods typically focus on the gene and peak counts while ignoring the underlying genomic sequence at accessible sites. Here, we propose ComicGTN, an innovative computational framework that integrates single-cell multiomic data with DNA sequence information via enhanced graph transformer networks to accurately identify rare cell clusters. ComicGTN consistently outperforms nine state-of-the-art methods in identifying rare cells across multiple complex scenarios. In mouse breast cancer data, ComicGTN detects several functionally distinct immune subpopulations. In cerebral cortex of epilepsy patients, it uncovers oligodendrocytes undergoing particular differentiation states. For polycystic kidney disease patient–derived organoids, ComicGTN elaborates pathological pathways in a captured rare glomerular subgroup. Overall, ComicGTN accelerates the localization of disease-associated rare cell populations, facilitating the derivation of clinical insights in development and disease progression.

bioinfo.title: PertDiffBench: Benchmarking Diffusion Models for Single-Cell Perturbation Response Prediction
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models are increasingly used to predict transcriptional responses to perturbations, but whether they improve on simpler generative and representation-based baselines remains unclear. Existing evaluations often do not separate the effects of model architecture, input representation, biological context and metric choice, making it difficult to determine where diffusion-based methods are useful. Here we introduce PertDiffBench, a standardized benchmark for diffusion-based transcriptomic perturbation prediction across single-cell and bulk RNA-seq datasets. PertDiffBench evaluates diffusion-based models across three complementary evaluation settings: standard prediction in known single-cell contexts and bulk perturbation conditions, generalization to unseen cell types, species, drugs and intermediate time points, and stress tests of feature dimensionality, input representation, noise type and gene ordering. Across these settings, diffusion models did not show a consistent advantage. scGen remained a strong baseline in common prediction tasks, whereas scDiffusion was the most competitive diffusion-based method in several generalization settings. Temporal imputation showed a different pattern, with a simple DDPM operating directly in expression space outperforming more specialized models. Stress tests showed that performance was model dependent and sensitive to feature dimensionality, encoder choice, noise type and gene ordering. Pretrained encoders did not consistently improve performance, with the classical scVI representation slightly exceeding STATE in seen-condition and unseen-cell-type settings. These results indicate that diffusion-model performance in perturbation response prediction depends strongly on task design and representation choice. PertDiffBench provides a practical framework for evaluating these models under biologically varied and stress-tested conditions.

ml.title: WorldLatent: A Unified 4D Latent Space for World Perception and Generation
ml.abstract: Generative Pre-Training (GPT) represents a profound milestone in natural language processing, serving as the foundation for most of today's state-of-the-art large language models. By casting diverse understanding and generation problems into a shared token representation, GPT enables a single architecture and unified optimization loop to master heterogeneous tasks across massive corpora, giving rise to powerful foundation models for natural language. In contrast, 4D spatiotemporal vision lacks a common representational protocol: perception (such as depth and camera estimation) and generation are either handled by separate one-way pipelines or bolted together from unaligned single-modality spaces. In this work, we introduce WorldLatent, a framework that formulates a unified 4D latent space as a common protocol for both world perception and generation. Rather than relying on fragmented, task-specific models or stacked single-modality representations, our framework proposes a multimodal VAE architecture that compresses and fuses complex 4D visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into a single structured latent representation. Within this formulation, perception and generation operate as complementary denoising processes over the same latent space, enabling one generative model to learn both capabilities simultaneously within a single training loop. Experiments across representative 4D benchmarks verify that our fused latent protocol achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent 4D generation, and controllable editing from a single model. By demonstrating that diverse 4D tasks can be seamlessly unified under a shared representational protocol, our work provides a scalable foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.

ml.title: TriageRAG: Failure-Aware Self-Training for Adapting Retrieval-Augmented Language Models to Specialized Domains
ml.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets large language models (LLMs) answer knowledge-intensive questions from retrieved evidence, but adapting a general-purpose RAG system to a specialized domain such as medicine is difficult when only an unlabeled corpus is available. Self-training approaches such as SimRAG address this by letting the LLM write its own question-answer pairs from domain passages and fine-tuning on the pairs that survive a round-trip consistency filter. We observe that these approaches treat every retained example identically: they never ask whether the student already knows the answer, already extracts it correctly from the retrieved context, or fails - and if so, whether the failure lies with the reader or with the retriever. To tackle this, we propose TriageRAG, a failure-aware self-training approach that probes the student on each self-generated question with and without retrieved context, triages it into one of four categories (known, solved, context-failure, retrieval-failure), and routes each category to the training signal that addresses it, including a parametric route that teaches the reader to answer when retrieval misses. Probing is cheap and repeated every round, so the training mixture follows the student, and the triage histogram doubles as a label-free diagnostic of where the domain gap lies. Experiments on 11 datasets spanning three domains with a Qwen3-4B backbone, and on CS-Bench with Qwen3-8B, demonstrate that TriageRAG outperforms a budget-matched SimRAG by 1.2-6.4 points and is the only method that recovers the closed-book level in every case where retrieval hurts the base model. A single ablation identifies the mechanism: round-trip filtering removes every training context that lacks the evidence, and a reader that never sees such contexts learns to over-trust noisy retrieval.

ml.title: Generating Samples of Stationary Distributions of Weakly Interacting Diffusion Models without Finite Particle Truncation: A Weak Generative Approach
ml.abstract: Computing the stationary probability density and generating corresponding samples for the mean-field model of an infinite number of weakly interacting diffusion particles pose significant numerical challenges, particularly in the phase transition regime where the interchangeability of infinite-time and infinite-particle limits breaks down. Traditional approaches, such as direct simulation of finite-particle systems, often fail to accurately pinpoint multiple stationary distributions in the mean-field meta-stable setting. On the other hand, solving the high-dimensional McKean-Vlasov partial differential equation using neural networks typically yields only the density function, limiting its utility for estimating statistical quantities from generating samples. In this work, we propose a novel generative framework based on the weak PDE formulation of the mean-field model to address these challenges. Our approach simultaneously computes the stationary distributions of McKean-Vlasov processes and generates independent and identically distributed samples that satisfy these distributions. This integrated approach not only reveals the true stationary distributions without the random perturbation of finite particle truncation, but also offers deeper insight into the system’s behavior in the mean‑field limit. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, showcasing its ability to accurately approximate stationary distributions, capture intricate phase transitions, and handle high-dimensional complex systems.

ml.title: One-Prompt Censorship Evasion via Generative Diffusion Models
ml.abstract: The escalating arms race between Internet censorship and evasion has driven censors to evolve from static rule-based filtering to sophisticated deep learning-based traffic analysis. While recent automated evasion tools have attempted to counter this by leveraging stochastic search and programmable heuristics, they continue to suffer from insufficient evasion robustness across diverse censorship modalities and poor usability due to complex, mechanism-specific configurations that require manual fitness tuning or domain-specific languages. In this paper, we propose a paradigm shift that reframes censorship evasion as a semantic image-to-image editing task, allowing users to execute it with a single prompt. We introduce FlowPaint, a novel generative framework that adapts large pretrained diffusion models to automatically reshape censored traffic into benign patterns. FlowPaint utilizes an instruction-tuned diffusion architecture to perform semantic editing on network flows. Evaluations against both industrial-grade rule-based middleboxes and learning-based classifiers demonstrate that FlowPaint outperforms existing censorship evasion baselines, enabling users to counter diverse censorship paradigms solely by varying natural language instructions.
ml.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Networking

ml.title: HOSE: Hierarchical Orthogonal Subspace Erasure for Concept Unlearning in Diffusion Models
ml.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can generate harmful or sensitive content, such as pornographic or violent imagery, raising serious security concerns. Model editing has recently emerged as an efficient approach to mitigate this issue. It modifies pretrained models with minimal parameter updates to alter specific concepts while preserving overall model capabilities. However, due to the entangled representations of different concepts in diffusion models, direct modifications inevitably disrupt non-target concepts. Meanwhile, U-Net's hierarchical heterogeneity hinders unified strategies from balancing erasure and quality. To address these issues, we propose Hierarchical Orthogonal Subspace Erasure (HOSE). This method projects parameter updates into the subspace orthogonal to general knowledge, thereby eliminating interference with non-target concepts. Considering the hierarchical heterogeneity of the U-Net architecture, we further propose a hierarchical adaptive mechanism, constructing differentiated subspace projections for different layers to precisely adapt to the model's hierarchical structure, thereby resolving the inherent trade-off between erasure and image quality in unified constraints. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method reduces harmful content generation by 80% compared with the unedited model. While it inevitably incurs some image quality degradation, it still outperforms other editing-based baselines in terms of quality preservation, and achieves a significantly better trade-off between harmful content suppression and quality loss than these baselines. Notably, our approach demonstrates higher adversarial robustness than existing SOTA method, indicating that the target concepts have been more thoroughly erased. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/sevenqiiu/HOSE.

ml.title: Generative structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model for MR to CT image synthesis in radiotherapy planning
ml.abstract: Objective . Radiotherapy (RT) planning uses magnetic resonance (MR) imaging for soft tissue information, while computerized tomography (CT) imaging is necessary for dose calculation. Synthetic CTs generated from MR images (MRI) streamline the clinical workflow by reducing the need for an actual CT acquisition while minimizing radiation exposure, enabling adaptive RT workflows. The objective of this study is to propose a new RT planning model combining stable structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) with MRI conditioning, for generating synthetic CT (sCT) images. Approach . The model combines a hybrid network architecture with a dynamic guidance mechanism, conditioned on MR images, to direct the reverse diffusion process and preserve structural details. The model integrates both a denoising and a refinement network: the denoising network predicts and progressively removes the noise added during the forward diffusion process, while the guidance strength adapts at each timestep based on the noise level. This adaptive guidance mechanism uses a non-linear formulation that satisfies noise constraints, optimizing the denoising process while preserving structural integrity. The training process includes a weighted structure-guided loss function that combines the DDPM noise loss with a dynamic guidance regularizer term for sCT image generation via noise prediction, along with a reconstruction loss for refinement. Main results . Evaluated on three paired MR/CT datasets (head and neck (HaN), as well as brain), our model outperforms recent MR to CT synthesis models, showing the best performance in image quality based on the mean absolute error in Hounsfield units, as well as improved peak signal-to-noise ratio, structural similarity index and gradient magnitude similarity deviation compared to other DDPM and generative adversarial network approaches. When comparing tumor segmentation quality, it achieves the best results in Dice score (0.76 ± 0.04), Hausdorff distance (7.9 ± 2.0), intersection over union (0.69 ± 0.04), geometric consistency index (0.84 ± 0.04) and precision-recall index (PRI) (0.88 ± 0.03) for segmented tumor regions in the generated sCT images. Finally, it achieves the best mean square error of 10.1 ± 2.6 Gray (Gy) in the head-and-neck cohort, when evaluating dose planning on sCT, with a conformity index of 0.61 ± 0.02 and a homogeneity index of 0.10 ± 0.02. Significance . Performance shows promise in integration for RT in HaN, as well as in brain cancers.

ml.title: ScanFlow: Context-Aware Fixation Transition Flow Matching for Generative Scanpath Prediction
ml.abstract: Scanpath prediction aims to generate realistic fixation sequences conditioned on visual scenes and tasks, capturing human visual attention. Recent studies model inherent gaze variability using generative techniques, particularly diffusion models. While effective, existing methods treat scanpath generation as modeling of holistic sequence distributions, in which contextual information is used as a conditioning signal rather than explicitly embedded in fixation sequences. This formulation overlooks that scanpaths are inherently composed of spatial-temporal, context-dependent fixation transitions, which may limit fine-grained coherence. To address this limitation, we propose a fixation-level generative paradigm for scanpath prediction. Unlike existing methods that capture coarse global structures, we model scanpaths as sequential fixation transitions, enabling fine-grained dependency and dynamic modeling across fixations, thereby naturally balancing coherence and variability. Specifically, we introduce a new framework, ScanFlow, with three key components. First, we integrate spatial-temporal and contextual semantics to construct scanpath representations that capture transition dependencies to preserve coherence. Second, we use flow matching with semantics-aligned contrastive regularization to model stochastic transition dynamics, thereby capturing structured and context-aware variability. Third, we adopt a flexible autoregressive strategy that balances deterministic and stochastic components to sequentially generate diverse yet context-coherent fixation sequences. Extensive experiments across five datasets with various viewing scenarios demonstrate the effectiveness of ScanFlow for high-quality and realistic scanpath generation.
ml.venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

ml.title: Internal Guidance as a Sampling Method for Tilted Diffusion Models
ml.abstract: Reward guidance methods sample an exponential tilt of a base density using a diffusion model trained with only samples from the base distribution. Existing methods use what we call external guidance: additive terms in the drift or multiplicative terms on the transition probabilities. We propose internal guidance which leaves the output of the base denoiser unmodified and instead changes the point at which it is evaluated. For discrete distributions embedded in the hypercube $\{-1,1\}^{d}$, the denoiser of any linearly tilted density is exactly the base denoiser evaluated at a shifted and rescaled input. In practice the base denoiser is a neural network trained on noised samples of the base distribution. The required evaluation points for sampling the tilted density would be out-of-distribution for basic noising of the base distribution. We modify the training algorithm with random diagonal rescalings of the data, so that the denoiser network learns both in- and out-of-distribution evaluations of the denoiser relative to the base distribution. A single denoiser network samples binary reward tilts, class labels, and infilling with no fine-tuning and no external guidance term.

ml.title: CoLink: Global Compression and Knowledge Linking for Multi-Turn Dialogue Modeling
ml.abstract: Extracting salient information from long-horizon dialogue histories remains a significant challenge for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to the restricted context windows and efficient retrieval challenges. Current methods typically rely on history organization or local token-level optimization, suffering from information loss, retrieval redundancy, and myopic attention. Inspired by the view in cognitive science that dialogue constitutes sense-making and memory association, we propose CoLink, a framework that enhances LLMs' global context awareness in domain-specific multi-turn dialogues through information linking and compression. CoLink first clusters historical contexts into topic graphs to establish cross-semantic associations with external knowledge. Guided by the adaptive control of thought, it then retrieves and activates knowledge via synergizing semantic relevance and graph-structural topology. Crucially, to achieve effective compression of history and knowledge, we ground multi-turn dialogues in information theory and derive a principled optimization objective for extracting the core sense-making information. Coupled with a competitive slot mechanism, CoLink condenses the global context into dedicated memory and knowledge slots, efficiently distilling lengthy, redundant inputs into an extremely compact latent representation. Extensive empirical results on both public and our MMD datasets validate CoLink's superiority and generalizability in knowledge linking and sense modeling.

ml.title: Generative Modeling with Bayesian Sample Inference
ml.abstract: We present a novel view of diffusion-like generative modeling from the perspective of iterative Gaussian posterior inference. By treating the generated sample as an unknown variable, we formulate the sampling process in the language of Bayesian probability: at each step, a model predicts the unknown sample from our current belief state and we compute a posterior belief from that prediction. Based on this formulation, we propose the generative model Bayesian Sample Inference (BSI). In addition to a rigorous theoretical analysis, we show that our perspective includes Bayesian Flow Networks (BFNs) and that BSI and BFNs represent the two opposite ends of a range of isotropic hyper-priors over the initial belief state. In our experiments, we demonstrate that BSI improves sample quality over both BFNs and the closely related Variational Diffusion Models on ImageNet32 and ImageNet64, while achieving equivalent log-likelihoods on both datasets.

ml.title: EEG Decoding in Context: A Framework for Tuning-Free EEG Foundation Models
ml.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) decoding is a central route toward brain-computer interfaces for communication, rehabilitation, cognitive assessment, and neurological monitoring. Recent EEG foundation models have substantially advanced reusable signal representations, but their downstream use still typically requires a task-specific decoder, gradient-based adaptation, and validation-driven model selection. We investigate a complementary foundation-model paradigm based on in-context learning: labeled EEG recordings define the decoding task as context, and new recordings are predicted without updating model parameters. We first pair raw EEG features with a pretrained general-purpose in-context predictor. This direct formulation provides a promising starting point, but its performance remains limited and unstable and does not generalize reliably across EEG paradigms. We find that suitable context construction can address these limitations by improving the effective signal-to-noise ratio and exposing temporal and spatial structure. Building on this insight, we introduce a general framework that combines EEG-specific context construction with a frozen in-context predictor and a metric-based context adaptation mechanism, which matches each downstream task to an appropriate context representation without relying on validation data. Across ten datasets spanning seven EEG decoding paradigms, our method achieves the highest mean BAcc among eleven specialized and fine-tuned EEG baselines, without task-specific parameter updates or validation-based model selection. This framework provides a practical path toward tuning-free EEG foundation models in which adaptation is expressed through context rather than parameter updates.

ml.title: Learning Algorithm Hyperparameters for Fast Parametric Convex Optimization
ml.abstract: Abstract. We introduce a machine-learning framework to learn the hyperparameter sequence of first-order methods (e.g. , the step sizes in gradient descent) to quickly solve parametric convex optimization problems. Our computational architecture amounts to running fixed-point iterations where the hyperparameters are the same across all parametric instances and consists of two phases. In the first step-varying phase the hyperparameters vary across iterations, while in the second steady-state phase the hyperparameters are constant across iterations. Our learned optimizer is flexible, in that it can be evaluated on any number of iterations and is guaranteed to converge to an optimal solution. To train, we minimize the mean square error to a ground truth solution. In the case of gradient descent, the one-step optimal step size is the solution to a least squares problem, and in the case of unconstrained quadratic minimization, we can compute the two-step and three-step optimal solutions in closed form. In other cases, we backpropagate through the algorithm steps to minimize the training objective after a given number of steps. We show how to learn hyperparameters for several popular algorithms: gradient descent, proximal gradient descent, and two ADMM-based solvers: OSQP and SCS. We use a sample convergence bound to obtain generalization guarantees for the performance of our learned algorithm for unseen data, providing both lower and upper bounds. We showcase the effectiveness of our method with many examples, including ones from control, signal processing, and machine learning. Remarkably, our approach is highly data-efficient in that we only use 10 problem instances to train the hyperparameters in all of our examples.
ml.venue: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science

ml.title: Bridging Generative and Discriminative Noisy-Label Learning via Direction-Agnostic EM Formulation
ml.abstract: Although noisy-label learning is often approached with discriminative methods for simplicity and speed, generative modeling offers a principled alternative by capturing the joint mechanism that produces features, clean labels, and corrupted observations. However, prior work typically (i) introduces extra latent variables and heavy image generators that bias training toward reconstruction, (ii) fixes a single data-generating direction (Y →X or X →Y), limiting adaptability, and (iii) assumes a uniform prior over clean labels, ignoring instance-level uncertainty. Here, we propose a single-stage, EM-style framework for generative noisy-label learning that is direction-agnostic and avoids explicit image synthesis. First, we derive a single Expectation Maximization (EM) objective whose E-step specializes to either causal orientation without changing the overall optimization objective. Second, we replace the intractable p(X | Y) with a dataset-normalized discriminative proxy computed using a discriminative classifier on the finite training set, retaining the structural benefits of generative modeling at much lower cost. Third, we introduce Partial-Label Supervision (PLS), an instance specific prior over clean labels that balances coverage and uncertainty, improving data-dependent regularization. Across standard vision and natural language processing (NLP) noisy label benchmarks, our method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, lower transition-matrix estimation error, and substantially less training computation than current generative and discriminative baselines. Code: https://github.com/lfb-1/GNL.

ml.title: Generative Modeling of Lévy Area for High Order SDE Simulation
ml.abstract: Abstract. It is well known that when numerically simulating solutions to stochastic differential equations (SDEs), achieving a strong convergence rate better than [Formula: see text] (where [Formula: see text] is the step-size) usually requires the use of certain iterated integrals of Brownian motion, commonly referred to as its “Lévy areas,” However, these stochastic integrals are difficult to simulate due to their non-Gaussian nature. and for a [Formula: see text]-dimensional Brownian motion with [Formula: see text], no fast almost-exact sampling algorithm is known. In this paper, we propose LévyGAN, a deep-learning-based model for generating approximate samples of Lévy area conditional on a Brownian increment. Due to our “bridge-flipping” operation, the output samples match all joint and conditional odd moments exactly. Our generator employs a tailored graph neural network (GNN)-inspired architecture, which enforces the correct dependency structure between the output distribution and the conditioning variable. Furthermore, we incorporate a mathematically principled characteristic-function-based discriminator. Lastly, we introduce a novel training mechanism, termed “Chen-training,” which circumvents the need for expensive-to-generate training data-sets. This new training procedure is underpinned by our two main theoretical results. For four-dimensional Brownian motion, we show that LévyGAN exhibits state-of-the-art performance across several metrics which measure both the joint and marginal distributions. We conclude with a numerical experiment on the log-Heston model, a popular SDE in mathematical finance, demonstrating that a high-quality synthetic Lévy area can lead to high order weak convergence and variance reduction when using multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC).
ml.venue: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science

ml.title: Mirror Descent at the Edge of Stability
ml.abstract: In many deep learning settings, gradient descent has been shown to operate at the edge of stability -- a regime where the largest eigenvalue of the loss Hessian hovers around $2/η$. We study this phenomenon in mirror descent, a generalization of gradient descent. As mirror descent is non-Euclidean, existing explanations of the edge of stability phase do not extend to this setting. We generalize the existing notion of sharpness to introduce mirror sharpness, which measures the curvature of the loss with respect to the mirror potential. Empirically, we observe that the mirror sharpness hovers slightly above the $2/η$ threshold. Furthermore, we derive a dual central flow ODE for mirror descent that models iterates in continuous time at the onset of edge of stability. Our ODE provides insights into the difficulties of extending existing arguments for why sharpness stabilizes at $2/η$ from gradient descent to mirror descent in full generality.

ml.title: Bridging Efficiency and Scalability in Generative Modeling
ml.abstract: Generative modeling has progressed from adversarial frameworks to diffusion and flow-based processes that now achieve state-of-the-art results across many domains. As these models have grown more capable, they have also sharpened a practical tension: the methods that deliver the highest quality often demand substantial cost in training, sampling, or deployment. We argue that the tradeoff between efficiency (strong results at lower computational cost) and scalability (improved quality with additional computation) is not absolute. Across six contributions spanning adversarial, diffusion, and flow-based models, we show that, although these objectives are often treated as competing, better objective design, inference-time search, and distillation can in important settings make generative systems both more efficient and more scalable. The first part of the thesis develops efficient training formulations. In adversarial generative modeling, we show that standard discriminator objectives exhibit alignment instability: the generator receives nonzero gradients even when it has already matched the data distribution, causing unnecessary oscillation. We introduce pairwise discriminators that eliminate this failure mode by making the aligned state stationary regardless of discriminator quality. We further develop Adversarial Support Alignment, replacing full distribution matching with the weaker but sufficient objective of support matching for domain adaptation under label shift. Turning to diffusion models, we introduce the Stable Target Field, which replaces the single-sample score estimation target with an importance-weighted average over a reference batch, substantially reducing target variance at high noise levels and accelerating convergence. We also present PFGM++, a unified framework connecting diffusion and Poisson flow models through a tunable augmented dimension that controls the tradeoff between training ease and sampling robustness. The second part introduces Inference-Time Scaling for diffusion models. We show that generation quality can continue to improve even after the gains from additional denoising steps have largely saturated by formulating inference as a search problem: candidate noises and trajectories are evaluated with learned verifiers, and test-time compute yields further quality gains. This establishes a new scaling axis for diffusion models, parallel to recent work on test-time compute in large language models. The final part bridges efficiency and scalability through distillation. While inference-time search produces high-quality outputs, it is too costly for practical deployment. We present FreeFlow, a data-free method for distilling flow models that addresses what we term Teacher-Data Mismatch: the gap between the data-noised intermediates used in standard distillation and the distributions encountered along the teacher's actual generating trajectories. By anchoring distillation at the prior (the unique point where these two processes must agree) and training through a predictor-corrector framework, FreeFlow distills the teacher into a single-function-evaluation student and achieves state-of-the-art one-step results without external data. The resulting model can also serve as a fast proxy for inference-time search, showing how efficient distillation can make scalable inference more practical. Together, these contributions show that efficiency and scalability in generative modeling need not always oppose one another: better formulations can improve stability and robustness, inference-time search can convert additional compute into better outputs, and efficient distillation can make those gains practical.

ml.title: SympFormer: Inertial Attention Blocks from Damped Hamiltonian Dynamics on Spaces of Probability Measures
ml.abstract: The attention mechanism underpins modern large language models, yet their dynamics remain only partially understood. Recent perspectives interpret attention blocks as interacting particle systems, whose mean-field limits correspond to gradient flows of energy functionals on spaces of probability densities on $\mathbb R^d$ equipped with Wasserstein-type metrics. We extend this viewpoint by deriving accelerated attention blocks from inertial, Nesterov-type damped Hamiltonian dynamics on these density spaces, developing the geometry and differential calculus needed to make the construction rigorous. In particular, we introduce a local-mobility geometry for the Otto-Wasserstein and softmax-Wasserstein settings, and a quotient Stein geometry that resolves the degeneracy of the linear-attention kernel to yield a well-defined metric and differential calculus. We provide rigorous foundations when softmax attention admits a gradient-flow formulation and when its inertial counterpart admits a damped Hamiltonian on explicitly characterized domains. For linear attention, we obtain a finite-dimensional solution theory with sharp conditions for global existence versus finite-time second-moment blow-up. We further prove a quantitative link between continuous moment blow-up and the discrete-layer depth at which token norms cross a prescribed threshold. Finally, motivated by the finite-token geometry, we propose geometric corrections to token and momentum updates. In decoder-only, nanoGPT-style experiments on TinyStories and OpenWebText, these corrections lower validation negative log-likelihood on next-token prediction relative to momentum-only controls.
